<FONT FACE=arial,helvetica><FONT SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">For those of us on this side of the pond who watch FOX-
News, we were entertained last night with a brief discussion of Rendlesham on "The
Factor".&nbsp; After all the tease throughout the show, I sort of expected to see Ian
Ridpath, James Easton, Jenny Randles, David Clarke, or Andy Roberts discussing the
matter.&nbsp; However, the one individual who was presented talking about the
"newly released" documents was Peter Robbins.&nbsp; Needless to say, I couldn't
believe it.&nbsp; Chris Gibson really demonstrated no preperation for the brief
interview and Robbins was able to say anything (stating there were three nights vice
two to include Larry Warren and, of course, plugging the book).&nbsp; If I recall
correctly, Col. Halt stated that Warren was never involved with the incidents in
question.&nbsp; It was too that somebody with a firmer grasp on the case conducted
the interview or had been included in on the debate.&nbsp; <BR>
<BR>
Tim Printy</FONT>

From: TPrinty@aol.com [mailto:TPrinty@aol.com]
Sent: Monday, July 23, 2001 16:13Subject: Re: [UFORL] Triangular Aircraft?


Steve wrote:

"Did you see the video of the one that flew over New Jersey last week?
Another night
sighting but it looked like a large flying triangle."

Steve, I think you are greatly mistaken about this event. All indications
are were that these were more than likely "flare balloons". There is no
indication of the lights being conected to a larger object. They slowly
drifted in the direction of the wind. It was highly localized. Most
important are some of the comments of the witnesses. For instance:

"As they were moving, a light would "drop" a "new" light
from it (less intense than itself) and the "new" light would
fade away. Immediately after that, the light that just
"dropped" the new light would also fade out. This happened
about five times as the collection of lights continued to move."

I am sure Larry Robinson recognizes this description.

Tim Printy

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 26 Jul 2001 00:50:49 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] July 14-15 Orange Lights over New Jersey

* Posted on behalf of Bob Young (who is still a subscriber) *

Ladies & Gents:

A letter from this past Sunday's Star Ledger (NJ) may shed some
real light on the July 14-15 mystery lights which received
widespread publicity in the Eastern U.S.

   "Logical Explanation"
   When I heard about the mysterious lights in Carteret, the
first thing I did was call my husband because he works at a data
center there. I figured maybe he would have a clue as to what the
mystery was about.
   Maybe he was the only one with a grip on reality. According
to my husband, the lights were nothing more than a group of
planes approaching the airport (Newark Airport, one on the 3 big
in NYC area-WTH) slowly and quietly. He said the planes flew by
while he was smoking a cigarette outside the building. He too
was intrigued by the mysterious lights when he first saw them,
but when they flew over the data center it became clear the
lights were airplanes.
   Human imagination is quite amusing. Perhaps some people need
drama in their lives. Maybe some lives are just so boring that
people need to fabricate stories about UFO's. The evidence is
clear. Let's be logical
   Carol Giroux, Edison"

I had earlier suggested that the lights may have been New Jersey
Army or Air National Guard aircraft dropping flares. This was a
Saturday night on a summer weekend. I think that it may be that
our old friends, "the Martians" or their colleagues, may be
flying some ultralights.

Clear skies,
Bob Young

<<
The general idea seems to be the objects drifted with the wind towards the

http://co-ops.nos.noaa.gov/data_res.html - I used Bergen Point West Reach
and Sandy Hook for the time in question). This means the wind was blowing

You may be right about the answer to this incident. In support

distant horizon. I also consider the possibility of ultralights,
but fire balloons might be more likely.

Clear skies,
Bob Young

<HTML><FONT FACE=arial,helvetica><FONT SIZE=2>List,
<BR>
<BR>There are some reports on the NIDS website
<BR>(http://www.nidsci.org/news/newjersey/intro.html). &nbsp;When placed along
with
<BR>the other reports listed in Filer's files and the news media, a picture is
<BR>beginning to form.
<BR>
<BR>1. &nbsp;There were 15-30 lights that were independent of each other over
Carteret
<BR>NJ at roughly 12:30 AM on the morning of the 15th. &nbsp;They were
independent
<BR>from each other since most witnesses do not report seeing the dark shape that
<BR>Filer keeps talking about. &nbsp;They also were reported in different
<BR>formations/formations that shifted.
<BR>
<BR>2. &nbsp;Direction of travel seems to have been to the East(Some witnesses at
NIDS
<BR>seemed confused about their directions). &nbsp;The NIDS interviewers were
not very
<BR>good at "fleshing out" the impotant details such as this. &nbsp;The easterly
<BR>direction was in the same direction as the wind.
<BR>
<BR>3. &nbsp;The color of the lights seemed to be amber/yellowish/gold.
<BR>
<BR>4. &nbsp;Almost all witnesses described the lights as simply "fading away" or
<BR>"disappearing". &nbsp;Several described small lights leaving the main light
prior
<BR>to it disappearing (witness #2 and #7 on NIDS). &nbsp;One witness (#3 on
NIDS)
<BR>reports seeing smoke.
<BR>
<BR>5. &nbsp;Duration was about 5-15 minutes for most witnesses.
<BR>
<BR>Compare these remarks to those from the Condon report Case 18. &nbsp;
<BR>
<BR>1. &nbsp;&nbsp;Triangular formations were reported. &nbsp;Others reported a
straight line.
<BR>
<BR>2. &nbsp;&nbsp;Motion was in the direction of the wind.
<BR>
<BR>3. &nbsp;The color of the lights seemed to be orange/redish/gold.
<BR>
<BR>4. &nbsp;Witnesses described the lights as "fading away" or "disappearing".
&nbsp;Two
<BR>of nine saw "sparks" leaving the lights
<BR>
<BR>5. &nbsp;Duration was about 5-15 minutes for most witnesses.
<BR>
<BR>Also note Hendry's remarks concerning prank balloons:
<BR>
<BR>"The important symptom of burning, dripping candle wax and conformance to
<BR>wind direction prevail here." &nbsp;(The UFO Handbook 47-8)
<BR>
<BR>Interesting parallels in these cases that should not be ignored. &nbsp;Also
<BR>interesting to note is Hendry's remarks about positively identifying the
<BR>source:
<BR>
<BR>"Only once did I ever have the luck of finding out exactly who launched one
<BR>and then only because the police caught him." (The UFO Handbook 47)
<BR>
<BR>While, the "garbage bag balloon" hypothesis is not proven (and may never be
<BR>based on Hendry's remark), it seems to be the most likely source of the
<BR>lights that evening.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 27 Jul 2001 03:32:16 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Triangular Aircraft?

Regarding:

>From: "Steve Douglass" <webbfeat@1s.net>
>To: <UFORL@yahoogroups.com>
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Triangular Aircraft?
>Date: 23 July 2001 18:11

Steve wrote:

>James, although your friend's sighting at close range is one I'd
>wish I had, it does not go without precendent. I witnessed three
>large triangular aircraft hovering (Harrier style) over the end
>of the main runway at Holloman, AFB in 1997 which bear striking
>simularities to the report you just cited.

Steve,

It's exceptionally interesting to hear about this.

>The first thing that brought these aircraft to our attention was
>the deep sub-woofer like rumbling and pressure wave they emitted
>as they circled the area.

Comparatively, one aspect of Julia's claims was a 'downward
pressure', to an extent she could hardly focus.

>After monitoring them working the southern bombing ranges they
>returned to Holloman to bed down for the night. We watched
>incredulously when while on final approach the trio suddenly
>stopped in mid-air and hovered.

This is all beginning to make some sense of several 'flying
triangle' reports that I considered credible.

>They slowly bobbed up and down for five minutes at the end of
>the runway.

>One by one each aircraft sped up and landed.

Amazing... sounds like an episode of the 'X-Files'!

>I have video that some day soon I'll post on my site.

That would be wonderful to see.

>As for these things just disapearing, the Pentagon has perfected
>day-time active camouflage. Check out the article I wrote on
>this for Popular Science on my web page.

I didn't consider the _apparent_ 'cloaking' and 'decloaking' as
far-fetched. I was aware of the overall history mentioned in your
article.

Still, if this was day-time camouflage and effective at such
close range in 1993/94, that was impressive and we can only
speculate how much more advanced it would be by now.

For information, the article by Steve and Bill Sweetman can be
read at:

http://www.projectblack.net/popsci2.html


>Since your friend lives near Edwards I wouldn't doubt for a
>second she saw something secret.

It was never an issue that Julia believed the craft was from
outer space, indeed, as she noted, "I'm used to seeing the
stealth planes, even when they denied the existence of them.
Those looked like giant bats in the distant sky. This triangular
craft was the same color as the stealth planes, which leads me to
believe they are experimental military planes".

Could well be that she was spot on!

Overall, a fascinating development to learn about your own,
similar 'UFO' sighting.

I'll pass details on to Julia and presuming her account is
genuine and factually reliable - as with any anecdotal testimony
that must be taken on trust, plus an assessment of the likely
credibility - I'm sure she will be pleased to finally have at
least the basis of an explanation for her 'close encounter'.


>Wish she had a camera!

This engages an intriguing facet of 'black project' research.

If Julia had obtained a clear, detailed photograph of the
'aircraft' and both you and I had a copy, what would you do with
it?

I would expect to be so concerned about compromising, if not
betraying, a conceivably vital military advantage of the 'free
world', that I doubt a million dollars would secure publication
of my photograph.

I can't say for certain, without someone actually offering a
million dollars versus my conscience.

The inherent question which has always been of interest is where
does any 'black project' revelation draw that proverbial line?


As a complete aside, there were a couple of USAF 'patches' which
Joel Carpenter kindly made available on this list's predecessor
and they can be seen at:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/patch1.jpg
http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/patch2.jpg

Have you come across them before?


James Easton.
E-mail: voyager@ufoworld.co.uk
www.ufoworld.co.uk

number of "15 to 30" objects as you suggest and then conclude
them to be garbage bag balloons. 15 to 30 of them is a fair
amount of work to launch. Do you know if there has been any
previous test to show the feasibility of one person putting these
things up there?

Please recall a similar event in Illinois recently and I had
wondered then about a team of hoaxers conspiring to pull of a
stunt of this sort, thinking an affair of this magnitude "too
involved" for one routine trickster. But if this event is taking
place in other localities, it would rule out the 'regional team'
and seem to suggest a nationwide network of tricksters.
Conspiratorial, I suppose, but not impossible.

I say again, putting one of these things up there is fairly
involved. And further, I don't think a simple 'candle in a bag'
would show up as vividly as seen in the videotapes from New
Jersey. These things are glaring with a brightness comparable (at
least) to an average streetlight to be picked up with consumer
videocameras. Distant garbage bag balloons floating about would
mostly give off a faint, spooky glow that should not generally be
visible to the routine consumer videocamera.
Further, I am not aware of any reports indicating the lights
'ascending' upwards - a trait that should be noted after the fire
balloons are launched. Further still, wouldn't they seem to
'congeal' from a certain launch point, rather than be staggered
about? Granted this could also be complicated by wind conditions,
observation locality, etc., but one would surmise that the
balloons would all be sort of 'centralized' around one sloppy
area. The video suggests otherwise.

In Middletown, Ohio during the summer of '96, a trickster put up
a roadflare suspended underneath an elaborate balloon
contraption. No smoke was seen on this one and the brilliant
red-colored flare was seen for miles, police chased it - much
action. But a privately owned airplane was instructed to
investigate by a tower operator at the airport nearby and he
approached it close, seeing the flare suspended from underneath
some sort of sophisticated balloon contraption. So it was a hoax
(identified by the pilot), but the idea could have been a part of
or the inspiration behind all these other things going on, but I
doubt it's a garbage bag balloon. More likely a series of burning
flares suspended from balloons. But I still opt for the 'military
flare' theory at this point...

Take care,
KENNY YOUNG

>> As for these things just disapearing, the Pentagon has perfected
>> day-time active camouflage. Check out the article I wrote on
>> this for Popular Science on my web page.
>
> I didn't consider the _apparent_ 'cloaking' and 'decloaking' as
> far-fetched. I was aware of the overall history mentioned in your
> article.
>
> Still, if this was day-time camouflage and effective at such
> close range in 1993/94, that was impressive and we can only
> speculate how much more advanced it would be by now.
>
> For information, the article by Steve and Bill Sweetman can be
> read at:
>
> http://www.projectblack.net/popsci2.html



This stuff --- requires as much skeptical attention as any UFO account IMO.
I could believe that underside lighting effects could be useful camouflage
under certain conditions (to help reduce shadows), but this business of
covering the whole _top_ of an aircraft with EL material that somehow mimics
the terrain below??? Come on, for the amount of weight and power consumption
this would require, could they justify such a thing as a countermeasure for
planes _above_ it? How often would an adversary be looking down at these
things under daylight conditions anyway? Could it possibly be bright enough
under real-world conditions to truly blend into the background as it moves?
If you think about this for about ten seconds you'll see how ludicrous the
idea is -- if the upper surface of the plane is replicating the terrain
directly below it, then an adversary behind and above would see something
different from the terrain behind the aircraft from his POV -- and an
adversary at another angle might see a piece of "aircraft-shaped terrain"
flying against a _sky_ background -- verdict: typical "black airplane
watcher" crap, along with Flying Artichokes, Antigravity B-2s, Donuts on
Ropes, and Aurora. But it makes great cover articles in "Popular
Pseudoscience" and "Hardwood Decks Illustrated," doesn't it?

Can the Black Airplane people pony up one single instance of an accurate
description of a real secret aircraft that's been declassified besides the
F-117?

Joel Carpenter

Absolutely. Military airplanes and their foes at ground or sea battle
stations do not have to _see_ each other to successfully engage, since
they use a device called _radar_ that was perfected many years ago...
To me, all this thing about "invisible" craft is just b*s*. Aside from
the impossibility of designing and building anything that actually works,
as Joel pointed out, the military gain that such technology would bring
would be nill. This reminds me about the crap related to the infamous
"Philadelphia Experiment" where an entire battle ship was supposedly made
"invisible". The story seems to be actually built upon a real experiment
in which strong magnetic fields where created around the ship in order
to prevent it from tripping magnetic mines. The ship was made invisible,
yes, but just to the mines...

probable that most people who would see or hear a military (or

way, and when hearing about a mass-UFO sighting later in the
evening (perhaps from a friend or in the news), might not even
equate the two.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Sat, 28 Jul 2001 04:16:39 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Triangular Aircraft?

Regarding:

>From: "joel carpenter" <ufx1947@home.com>
>To: <UFORL@yahoogroups.com>
>Subject: Re: [UFORL] Triangular Aircraft?
>Date: 27 July 2001 18:35

Joel wrote:

>This stuff --- requires as much skeptical attention as any UFO
>account IMO.

Joel,

Absolutely...

>Can the Black Airplane people pony up one single instance of an
>accurate description of a real secret aircraft that's been
>declassified besides the F-117?

How do we reconcile Chris Gibson's detailed observation - Chris
of course being an aircraft recognition expert - of that
triangular aircraft which has _never_ been declassified?

For those who aren't familiar with Chris's sighting report - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/chris_g.txt

As seemingly credible, related evidence, there's also that
possible 'faux pas' which occurred in the UK documentary 'Billion
Dollar Secrets', broadcast in 1999.

To recap; the documentary featured some research into US 'black
budget' programmes which was undertaken by Nick Cook, a British
aviation journalist and correspondent for 'Jane's Defence
Weekly'.

This included interviews with Jack Gordon, CEO of the 'Skunk-
Works' and Boyd Bushman, who works with 'advanced concepts' for
LockMart.

Perhaps the most significant and exceptional interview was with
Lt. Gen. George Muellner, who acknowledged that 'black projects'
are kept that way until they 'mature'.

The following is a transcript of discussions between Nick Cook
(NC) and 'General' Muellner (GM):

NC: General, I've just spent a couple of days in Southern
Colorado, where a lot of apparently credible witnesses are
reporting sightings of apparently unconventional aircraft, and I
mean things like huge black triangles, silent helicopters, all
kinds of extraordinary craft.

Should we be looking to the USAF for whatever is going on in this
place?

GM: Well, the only programmes that I'm aware of that we have
operating out in that environment... obviously are 117s operate
out of Holloman... they're triangular shaped, obviously they're
black and they operate at night quite frequently and so on.

All of the rest of the aeroplanes we have operating down in the
Holloman area in particular are all conventional airplanes.

So, I don't know of any other development programmes or anything
else that's going on down in that area or in southern Colorado in
general, or for that matter in the New Mexico area.

We don't have anything of significance operating there.

I can tell you as an aviator though, quite frequently it's very,
very difficult to discern what a platform is. B-2 for instance,
if you're looking near co-altitude with it, it just seems to
disappear into the background.


NC: But again, these people are describing things that literally
hover over them sometimes, seemingly unmistakable sightings of
these things.

GM: Well, I'll tell you, if they can get me the name of the
contractor and whosoever operating, I'd love to put them under
contract to develop some of these things.
[END]


When this program was subsequently shown in the US, someone made
an intriguing observation:

"I was watching a TLC program today called 'Billion Dollar
Secret' and something very interesting caught my eye.

Jane's Nick Cook was interviewing the head of the Air Force when
I began looking at the collection of models on the shelves behind
his head. Notice anything funny? On the left side of the screen
was an unidentifiable aircraft that looked remarkably like the
stealth swing wing 'switch blade' that I've been chasing for the
last few years.

Take a look at the attached frame grabbed stills and tell me what
you think?".


I couldn't recall who had spotted that conceivable clue, however,
when I, eventually, located my archived copy, it was no surprise
to find this originated from Steve Douglass.

I've also found a copy of that 'frame grab' and uploaded it to:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/swing.jpg


If I'm not mistaken, Chris commented that the 'non existent
aircraft' depicted was a close resemblance to what he had
observed.

I suppose the point is - what other developments have never been
revealed?

I do however share your due skepticism and still find it
difficult to accept that Julia's report - albeit
'straightforward' and seemingly credible - is evidence of an
overall remarkable technology which remains comprehensively
concealed.

Conversely... we have Steve's reported observation of those
'verging on unbelievable' 1997 Holloman, AFB 'black' aircraft.

Adding some proverbial fuel to the fire, Nick Cook states, "But
again, these people are describing things that literally hover
over them sometimes, seemingly unmistakable sightings of these
things".

And he wasn't even aware of Julia's account!


As a result of this discussion, I've been reminded of Muellner's,
quite fundamental, remarks:

"Well, I'll tell you, if they can get me the name of the
contractor and whosoever operating, I'd love to put them under
contract to develop some of these things".

It's a pity Nick Cook couldn't have asked... "that stealth swing-
wing 'switch blade'... who developed this aircraft, has its
existence been disclosed and is it operational?".

Muellner's response to _that_ would have been worth seeing!


I'm sure we can all agree on what must be an evident conclusion;
the truth is out there, and someone's not conveying it.


James Easton.

maneuvers. Now do we know why the overlap? That will always be
speculative.

Not necessarily and again speculative. Keep in mind the high

(compounded further still by direction of travel vs. observation
angle), also keep in mind the likeliness of jet aircraft

would project the flares and move off, and he expressed no great
surprise that others who would see the flares would mistake them
for UFOs. Localization and 'low level' does not necessarily
obfuscate the flare explanation. Everything is localized
somewhere and gravity dictates it coming down low in the long
run.

Assuming that the jets 'stick around' or hover in place after

From: Kenny Young <ufo@fuse.net>
Date: Sun, 29 Jul 2001 01:04:31 -0400
Subject: Re: [UFORL] July 14-15 Orange Lights over New Jersey

TPrinty@aol.com wrote:
>
> Kenny, curious that you should state the aircrafts MOA is
> between these two
> points. Do you have conclusive proof they were outside the MOA?

In the Ohio '97 case, flares and jets were directly overhead in
Wilmington, Ohio at low=level. This, as stated earlier, is
roughly 50 miles or more to the northeast of the Buckeye MOA.
Maysville, Kentucky is also not in a MOA and flares were reported
in this immediate area also. Evansville, Indiana from '98 is
another occasion.


> What you seem to be suggesting is that the aircraft that
> dropped these flares managed to fly
> overhead without anybody noticing.

I see no reason to require anyone to 'notice' the plane sounds
given the many variables such as elevation and how sound would
carry from a certain distance and certain pre-existing ambient
noise from their observation locality. I also see no reason to
require anyone to 'notice' the planes visibly from their distant
location as opposed to their movement, elevation and brightness
vs. the relatively stationary (w/slight descending barely
perceptible) motion of bright flares.

> Given that the number of supposed flares is 15-30, this
> would require more than one craft since the compliment of most
> aircraft would be less than this number. As for the exact
> number, I am not sure how many but one aircraft dropping
> flares for kicks just does not make sense.

I'm not with you on this one. I can't see anything that defies
reason to suppose three or four jets could have been out there
randomly maneuvering around and putting out flares.
Counter=arguments seem to presuppose things without taking into
account basic elements such as distance, angle of observation
plus the ever-present 'witness misperception' potential.


> This is the Stanley observation which goes a long way to
> explaining the
> 8-8:30 PM event and not the flare 10PM event. You seem to
> think that a
> military jet overflying an area dumping flares would go
> unnoticed. Newark
> does not have military jets frequenting the area. It would not
> be "routine".

And once again, this goes to show that a rare sort of event as
this one will generate UFO claims.


> So, even in areas where military jets were frequently seen,
> people did not
> "ignore" the aircraft. The low altitude of the NJ lights would
> imply the
> drop was made at low altitude and the witnesses in Carteret
> would have
> seen/heard the jet(s) passing by.
>

It wouldn't be practical to require the jets to 'stick around'
the flare once its burning, it also isn't necessary for every
witness, from their distant vantage point, to take note of the
jet by its running lights or hear its engine. The few cases where
they are observed in conjunction with the flares establishes
precedent for the viability of these operations but once again, I
see no reason to require the positive identification of jets in
conjunction with the flares they leave behind on every occasion.

Best regards,
KENNY YOUNG

From: Ed Stewart <ufoindex@lanset.com>
Date: Mon, 30 Jul 2001 12:05:30 -0700
Subject: [UFORL] Hugo Gernsback and Flying Saucers

Hugo Gernsback wrote a science fiction serial published in his
publication _The Electrical Experimenter_ in thirteen illustrated parts
from May 1915 to February 1917 entitled "Baron Münchhausen's New
Scientific Adventures". Each episode describes the Baron's _experiences_
and _observations_ on the Planet Mars and with Martians. The serial type
of story was popular since it was used to increase circulation and it
was widely adopted by the growing waves magazines including the pulps.
_The Electrical Experimenter_ cannot be described as a pulp since it was
printed on high quality paper. In the below episode:

  • Electrical Experimenter [v3 #11, March 1916] (large)
  • Baron Münchhausen's New Scientific Adventures: 9. The Cities of
Mars • Hugo Gernsback • ss

Gernsback described Martian cities. The illustration accompanying the
chapter shows a myriad of flying saucers over and around the Martian
city. Gernsback was to use flying saucers in both cover and internal
story illustrations throughout his publishing career which expanded
through the 1960s.

But this is not the earliest known use of a flying saucer in a Gernsback
publication. Jacques Sadoul's _Histoire de La Science Fiction Moderne_
shows a flying saucer on the cover of Gernsback's _Modern Electrics_
December 1911 issue. This same design was later used in the _Amazing
Stories Quarterly_ January 1929 issue and credited to illustrator Frank
Paul who had an enduring association with Gernsback's as his main cover
and story artist throughout his publications. Most early flying saucer
illustrations (pre-1947) I have come across are the artistry of Frank
Paul and are contained in Hugo Gernsback publications.

Could either/both actually be "The Father of Flying Saucers" in 20th
popular culture and thus have had a dominant cultural influence in the
lore of flying saucers?

Ed Stewart

From: Chris Gibson <cgibson@skomer.u-net.com>
Date: Mon, 30 Jul 2001 23:26:37 +0000
Subject: Re: Re: [UFORL] Triangular Aircraft?


The FAS had the best description of the Black aircraft phenomenum "...an
epistological exercise". I think the BAWs had their day back in the mid nineties. Their
bandwagon was jumped upon and collapsed like a sumo wrestler's deck chair. The
early stuff was good, but IMO last year's Aircraft Illustrated finally killed it dead. I
was looking for an Ali-G byline, everyone else seemed to get in on the act. Nobody
wants to know any more. I feel sorry for the guys who submitted work for that, I
suspect they were under the impression it was for a one-off sprint, rather than a 6
month marathon.

In the early nineties there was some very good work done, it was very tight and well
researched. Unfortunately a multitude of Aurora websites sprung up when the web
took off in 96, not so tight, not so well researched. This produced instant black aircraft
experts (I think long term subscribers know who I'm talking about) and looking more
and more like UFOlogy every day. I look at them very occasionally and despair of the
rubbish I read.

The main BAWs (unfortunate acronym, eh James?) from the early nineties have left
the scene, leaving it to the new generation. The chaps in the van now are the
specialists, who like yourself Joel, are researching particular aspects of the scene,
there is no smoke without fire and some of the best research is looking at the kindling
for these fires.

I came to the conclusion that black aircraft are like Schrodinger's cat. Until the lid is
lifted, we won't know what's going on. So why get excited about it?

I know what Joel is on about, ie when black aircraft do finally get revealed, they'll
look nothing like the pundits say. It is like building a jigsaw without the picture on the
box, the various pieces being gleaned from witness description and open sources for
technical aspects like powerplants or aerodynamics.

Shamu is interesting, no sooner had Curtis Peebles said it was a load of bollocks when,
ping! Up it popped, out of the black. Made my day.

Where did the description on Shamu come from? When I saw Tacit Blue I could see
where the Stratocruiser analogy originated. People describe unfamiliar aircraft with
reference to aircraft they know, this guy saw aspects of the Stratocruiser. Not a
Stratocruiser with B-2 wings as drawn in "Dark Eagles", but a style of cabin glazing. I
suspect a 1945 Luftwaffe pilot on seeing a B-29 would describe it as having a cockpit
like an Arado 234.

When it comes to black aircraft a lot of information is sifted to produce descriptions.
At the end of the day an editor wants a description and pays an expert to produce this
description. That's what they are paid for, to put their head above the parapet
(something I won't do). It's easy to sit back years later and pick holes in these
descriptions with 20/20 hindsight. I have a drawing of "Aurora" published in 1990. Its
teardrop shape seems to have sunk without trace. Could this be the true shape?

Also, as the situation evolves, so must the descriptions and drawings. That I would
suggest is a scientific approach.

I'd still want to kick the tyres.

Chris

From: Ed Stewart <ufoindex@lanset.com>
Date: Sat, 04 Aug 2001 12:40:33 -0700
Subject: [UFORL] Lindbergh, Jung and Keyhoe

The following is to be found in A. Scott Berg's _Lindbergh_, copyrighted
1998, a Pulitzer prize winner and New York Times bestseller biography of
Charles Lindbergh. The following passage took place according to Charles
Lindberg's wife Anne during a visit of the Lindberghs to Carl G. Jung's
home in July 1959:

---
        Jung abruptly changed the subject to flying saucers. "I had expected a
fascinating discussion about psychological aspects of the numerous and
recurring flying-saucer reports," Lindbergh later recorded. But he
found, to his astonishment, that Jung believed all the reports and was
no more interested in the psychology of the phenomenon than he was in
learning any facts about it. When Lindberg told him that the United
States Air Force had investigated hundreds of reported sightings without
finding a shred of evidence of supernatural phenomena, Jung indicated he
did not wish to pursue the discussion much further. He referred to a
book about flying saucers by Donald Keyhoe, the very pilot who had flown
alongside Lindbergh on his fory-eight-state tour of the United States in
1927, which reported numerous sightings of unidentified flying objects.
When Lindbergh said he had heard recently that Keyhoe had, in fact,
experienced several nervous breakdowns, Jung replied, "I dare say he
has."
        Lindbergh added that he had discussed with Chief of the United States
Air Force General Spaatz the recent flurry of UFO reports. "Slim,"
Spaatz had said, "don't you suppose that if there was anything true
about this flying-saucer business, you and I would have heard about it
by this time?" Jung was not impressed. "There are," he said, ending
their conversation, "a great many things going on around this earth that
you and General Spaatz don't know about."
---

Can anyone shed some insight regarding the "several nervous breakdowns"
that Donald Keyhoe allegedly experienced according to both C.G. Jung and
Charles Lindbergh and whether or not they were related to his work with
UFOs and NICAP? This is the first time I have read anything that Keyhoe
had nervous breakdowns.

Ed Stewart

There is a possibility that a very small minority of "black
triangles" are hang gliders. A couple of weeks ago i saw a black slow
moving triangular shaped object go behind some clouds. I was puzzled
about this for a while until it came out of the clouds and i could
see that it was in fact a hang glider. I could only hear the noise of
the hang glider when it was pretty much directly overhead. When i
first saw the hang glider in the distance it looked very strange. The
sun was shining on the hang glider and on the clouds in such a way
that it made it look quite unusual.

The point that i am trying to make here is that it is possible that
if someone were to see a black trianglar hang glider in the distance
for a very short time before it went behind some clouds then they may
believe that they have seen a UFO.

I would imagine that the wind would have to be blowing in a certain
direction so that they couldn't hear the engine as well but it is
possible.

When i first saw the object i didn't really have any idea of the size
or distance of it. Only when it came closer and i recognised what it
was could i figure out the distance.

From: "Robert McLean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>
Date: Sun, 5 Aug 2001 22:20:11 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 'Rendlesham' (and Col Halt's 2 lighthouses)

James

I think you're right that the drawing on page 141 of Sky Crash originates
from John Burrough' sketch, and so it has nothing to do with the explosion
of light seen by Col Halt.

However, I am sure that the explosion of light and the disappearance of the
UFO seen by Col Halt, really did occur. Before I explain why, just consider
how likely it is that Col Halt would have related the "explosion" story,
where the UFO appeared to have dispersed into five "white" lights (he never
claims he saw the actual dispersion), if he really had seen that same UFO
again in the second farmer's field. If he had seen that same UFO again in
the second farmer's field, wouldn't he also have related the even more
amazing story of how the previously "exploded" UFO appeared somehow to have
re-assembled itself?

At the beginning of the UFO chase, there are three separate references on
the Halt tape to a light seen at about 110 or 120 degrees.

At the end of the UFO chase, Col Halt says on the tape:

HALT: At two forty-four [2:44 am], we're at the far side of the farmer's . .
. the second farmer's field and made sighting again about 110 degrees. This
looks like it's clear off to the coast. It's right on the horizon. Moves
about a bit and flashes from time to time. Still steady or red in color.

In between these points on the Halt tape, the UFO appeared to explode,
although this is not documented on the tape.

Understanding what actually happened has been stymied for two reasons:

i) The location of the true landing site was incorrectly identified, in
particular by Col Halt to Brenda Butler on her OS map (Sky Crash p131). I
have seen this map
on which Col Halt wrote an "X" in pen, and he placed it in the area where
the Orfordness lighthouse can be seen, although about two hundred metres
further west (i.e. further from the eastern edge of the forest) than
generally accepted.

ii) The location of the second farmer's field was never positively
identified. Some people thought it might be at Butley Abbey, in low lying
ground where no lighthouse/ships can be seen.

When I studied an OS map looking for a likely location for the second
farmer's field where the Orfordness lighthouse might have been seen, my
first guess was Burrow Hill. I went to Burrow Hill at night, but couldn't
find any place where the lighthouse was visible. So I looked for another
place, and located a farmer's field a bit further south, just east of
Boyton, where there is a clear view of both Orfordness lighthouse, and the
location of the former Shipwash lightship. This turned out to be a big
mistake. I had fallen into the same trap as everyone else (except Steuart
Campbell) in assuming that it was the Orfordness lighthouse that Halt
initially followed at a compass heading of 110 to 120 degrees.

When I explained my theory to Brenda Butler she explained that it couldn't
be right because the second farmer's field was Burrow Hill. She said that
Col Halt had described to her the view in the second farmer's field as the
UFO in the south moved towards them at high speed. He described seeing the
line of a river in the moonlight stretching away to the south, with the UFO
following the line of that river. Col Halt did not know it was Burrow Hill,
or show it to her on a map, but Brenda realised that the description matched
Burrow Hill, which it surely does. Butley River runs past the east side of
Burrow Hill, and the hill is high enough so that river can be seen clearly
by moonlight. Halt's description did not match my initial identification of
the second farmer's field, and I realised I had to re-think things.

I suspected that the true landing site was not where Col Halt had placed it
on the map. In summary, the reasons for this are:

1. There was no plausible route from the accepted location to the second
farmer's field. A direct route involves crossing no fewer than eight
drainage ditches over a 2 km distance in the Butley and Stonebridge marshes
(1.5 m below sea level), some of which you would have to swim across.

2. The trees at the accepted location were far too tall to have had
branches
at 15 feet height, as described on the Halt tape.

3. Aerial photos show that in 1971 there was no clearing in the trees as
described by Burroughs and Penniston.

4. Col Halt described the path he took through the first farmer's field
as being on the left hand side of the field, and bearing towards the left
edge of the field (see You Can't Tell the People pages 271/2). Assumin he
was in the field just to the west of Capel Green, this path would have been
at a magnetic heading of about 70 degrees, not 110 or 120
degrees.

5. In a TV documentary, Col Halt says "The light was about, oh, 15 or 20
degrees off to our left, almost directly in front of a farmer's field." This
agrees with the description mentioned above from YCTTP. However, in the
field just to the west of Capel Green, Orfordness lighthouse is 5 degrees to
the right (assuming a baseline along the boundary between field and forest).

6. If we accept Halt's description of his path in the first farmer's
field (again see YCTTP pages 271/2) then the farmhouse on the left side of
this field is almost completely obscured by trees, and is also on the wrong
side of the road {

Source A: Internet page dealing with miracles. My

Text of source A:

“On December 17, 1826, after sunset, approximately
three thousand people gathered for a jubilee ceremony
at Migne, in the jurisdiction of Poitiers, France. All
three thousand witnessed a magnificent luminous object
shining "brighter than the sun" and "clearly not of
this world" in the open sky above them. Records of
this event indicate that the heavenly object resembled
a cross, but by its description it hardly seems
likely. The length of the celestial "cross" measured
forty feet and its cross-member measured about four
feet. The crowd was seized with excitement, and a
general feeling of brotherhood and unity prevailed
even long after the spectacle had vanished. Some wept,
some raised exclamations of wonder, some lifted their
hands to heaven, some studied and measured and
scrutinized and others simply took note. The reason
for this phenomenon has never been ascertained, as no
one among the witnesses has ever offered a single
reasonable insight.”

(Bibliothèque Marabout, Belgium 1977, p.86).

reproduce it here. See the following notes)

dans la nuit, “Mystérieuses soucoupes volantes,”
Albatros, 1973 p. 283.

Piens has “Migne-Auxances (near Poitiers)” for “Migne,
in the jurisdiction of Poitiers.” Which is more
correct?

Piens has “80 feet” instead of “forty feet and its
cross-member measured about four feet.” Which was the
correct measurement?

Piens adds that 200 people provided a (written? oral?)

Piens’ source: F. Largarde et le groupement Lumières

“We hear from Perthsire, that an uncommon phaenomenon
was observed on the water of Isla, near Cupor Angus,
preceded by a thick dark smoke, which soon dispelled,
and discovered a large luminous body, like a house on
fire, but presently after took a form something
pyramidal, and rolled forwards with impetuosity till
it came to the water of Erick, up which river it took
its direction, with great rapidity, and disappeared a
little above Blairgowrie. The effects were as
extraordinary as the appearance.

over a field of grass; a man riding along the high
road was carried from his horse, and so stunned with
the fall, as to remain senseless a considerable time.

behind, undermined and destroyed an arch of the new
bridge building at Blairgowrie, immediately after
which it disappeared.

with like consequences, various conjectures have been
formed concerning it.”

1. Official Documents Demolish 'UFO Cover Up' Absurdity.

Congratulations to Dr David Clarke on his acquisition of
previously unreleased Ministry of Defence [MoD] documentation

Dr Clarke has successfully obtained what seems to effectively be
the MoD's, apparently non-existent, 'Rendlesham forest UFOs'
file.

The contents are a landmark disclosure.

A highly commended new web site has been set up with freely
available copies of the main documents, at:

http://www.flyingsaucery.com/


Some have proclaimed the Ministry was involved in a 'UFO cover
up', part of that supposed nefarious and grandiose, global,
clandestine conspiracy.

However, it has long been evident to more objective researchers
of this most famous, British 'UFO' case, a pillar of such beliefs
world-wide, why its perceived 'UFO' evidence was fundamentally
flawed from the outset.

That fact is exemplified by the contents of this historic,
official 'UFO' file. All we find exposed here, within over 150
'secret' documents, is the specious foundation for any 'UFO cover
up' declarations.

It's now confirmed how the MoD did spend considerable time
investigating those purported 'Rendlesham forest UFOs'.


The forest separated RAF Bentwaters and RAF Woodbridge, a twin-
base complex, operated by the USAF. Deputy Base Commander, Lt.
Col. Charles Halt. had written to the Ministry regarding the
'UFO' events and their investigations centred on that memorandum.

There were two distinct 'UFO incidents' and it's comprehensively
established that Halt's memo contained the wrong dates.

The incidents occurred at circa 0300 on the morning of 26
December and the night/early morning of 27/28 December. Halt
erroneously reports the dates as 27 and 29/30 December
respectively.

The MoD file confirms this astonishing faux pas was a major
factor why their investigations focused on spurious data.

Incredibly, the MoD papers confirm it was 1983, when science
writer Ian Ridpath wrote to them, before they were even aware of
the true situation.


How could Halt have been so mistaken.

It's a question which I may be the only person ever to have
raised directly. During 1997, it was publicised that American
journalist Salley Rayl was to interview Halt and I enquired if
she would please ask some questions on my behalf.

The 13 May, 1997 transcript records:

RAYL: We received an e-mail earlier in the day from a fellow by
the name of James Easton who lives in Scotland and apparently has
been researching this case during recent months.

[...]

One thing that he mentioned and a question that I would like to
pass on to you is why have there been variances in the dates
given for both incidents? Your memo claims that the dates were on
the evening, early morning of the 26th, 27th and 28th, 29th of
December, respectively. But elsewhere, you know, the dates have
been given as 25 to 26 and 29 to 30, he says. So why, why are
there differences in those dates?
HALT: Well, I tried to go back and recover the police blotter and
the security blotter think I mentioned to you earlier to re-
affirm the dates. Keep in mind, I wrote the memo several weeks
later. And it was not a really important memo. The date was not
critical. The critical portion was, you know, what happened and
are you interested? And how about getting involved and let's
investigate this. It's possible that I, I put the date down
wrong. But I don't believe so. I tried to verify later and the
police blotters had been taken from repository, probably by a,
how shall I say, curiosity seeker...
[END]


Halt's memo was dated 13 January and the relevant background is
perhaps best explained in Halt's own words, from that same
interview:

RAYL: Okay. Now, two weeks later on January 13, 1981 you issued a
memorandum to the British Ministry of Defense.

HALT: That's correct.

RAYL: And why did you do that?

HALT: At the request of the R.A.F. Liaison Officer or the R.A.F.
Base Commander, as we called him, Don Moreland.

RAYL: Okay.

HALT: I went and approached him, and I said, "You know, this
happened off base." Well, I did discuss this through our channels
and the real answer from our channels was, "Hey, we don't want to
touch this with a pole. This was a British incident. It happened
off the installation. Let them handle it." So, I contacted him.
In fact, I contacted him earlier and the only reason the memo was
dated that late was that he was on vacation and I wasn't able to
find out what he wanted and how much detail he wanted and what he
wanted to do with the information. When I finally caught up with
him on the, about the 10th or the 12th, he said, "Well, write a
brief memo. Kind of sanitize it and we'll send it to London.
We'll see what happens." So, that's what I did.

RAYL: That memo is probably one of the most amazing documents
that's been released to the UFO community, I would say within the
last 20 years or so and while you never use the term UFO in it,
it reads like science fiction. When you were writing that, did
you get that sense at all, that what you're writing here may be
not taken entirely seriously?

HALT: Well, there was no intent for that to be released publicly.
That was, you know, not a classified document, as some people
have alluded to. It was given to Don Moreland to forward through
his channels which was that Liaison Officer, Third Air Force, Air
Force Headquarters in England, to the M.O.D. and see what their
interest was. I really expected somebody to pop up in a day or
two and want more details. To this day, it hasn't happened.

[...]

RAYL: ...You had the copy of the micro-cassette recording that
you made that night and that also found its way into the UFO
community when the story broke publicly with the release of the
memo... somebody said that the micro-cassette recording was
actually two hours long and it's always been my understanding
from you that it was closer to twenty minutes.

HALT: It's closer to twenty minutes. I've never timed it.

RAYL: Okay. So, there...

HALT: Because I turn the machine off when I wasn't actually
talking...

RAYL: Right.

HALT: ...In fact, some times I talked and I didn't record. You
know, I only recorded what I thought was pertinent.

RAYL: Okay. So when you had something to say, you'd hit the
record button and speak into it.

HALT: Keep in mind, this is the recorder I use when I traveled
around the base to record things I saw that needed [to be] fixed
or whatever, and I would normally just when I went around in a
staff car you know, make a recording. Talk from time to time.
Flick it on and off and then go back and thread the tape to the
secretary and say, "Here, put it on your dictating machine. Type
it up and we'll mark it for who the pertinent staff agency is
that should take action on these items." That's basically what I
did.

RAYL: Okay.

HALT: It was very common to carry the tape recorder with me. Sure
beats taking notes.

RAYL: Sure does. And how did that get released into the UFO
community? I think a lot of people would be interested in that.

HALT: I made a copy for my boss then, Ted Conrad. He wanted a
copy of it so I made a copy and when he rotated and was re-
assigned, he left it in the desk unbeknownst to me, and Sam
Morgan came in to replace him. Sam Morgan found it and asked me
what it was. I played it for him and he thought it was hilarious
and he gave a copy to a British solicitor in the UFO community
named Harry Harris who, in turn, sold, distributed, gave away,
etc., copies until they're all over the world.

[...]

HALT: The Wing Commander at that time was not present. ...He and
I discussed this incident the day after, which was a day or two
after which was a Saturday morning. I remember running into him
in the hallway of the building we shared a common office building
and I told him about it. He knew a little bit, but I told him
some details and told him I made the tape and he was very
interested and asked to hear the tape. I gave him the tape and
played it for him and he said, "May I take this to the Third Air
Force, to the staff meeting next Tuesday or Wednesday?" I said,
"Certainly." Well, I couldn't tell him, no. And he took it down
and played it to the staff and the General looked at the staff
and said, "First, the Wing Commander said, 'Is he a credible
witness?' and the answer was, 'Yes.' So he turned to the staff
and said, "What do we do now?" And nobody knew what to do. So
there was some chuckling in the room and I understand the comment
was, "Well, it's a British affair. Let's give it to them."

RAYL: And that's what you did?

HALT: And that's what everybody did. And I was told when he came
back, he gave me the tape back and thanked me and said, "Get with
Don Moreland. Let the British handle this."
[END OF EXTRACT]


Crucially, Halt clarifies that a senior General attended the
staff meeting. It seems a reasonable deduction this was General
Charles A. Gabriel, who was at that time Chief of Staff of the US
Air Staff and Commander in Chief of US Air Forces in Europe at
Ramstein AFB, Germany.

It would correlate with a letter contained within the MoD's
papers, when on 16 February 1981, Squadron Leader Badcock wrote
to them:

"I have spoken with Sqn Ldr Moreland at Bentwaters and he
considered the Deputy Base Commander [Halt] a sound source. I
asked if the incident had been reported on the USAF net and I was
advised that tape recorders of the evidence had been handed to
Gen Gabriel who happened to be visiting the station. Perhaps it
would be reasonable to ask if we could have tape recordings as
well."

I have a FOIA request that has been with Ramstein AFB for some
time now and which seeks to clarify a number of related issues.


Halt didn't take any witness statements until a full week
afterwards and states this delay was due to the holiday period.

Apparently, written testimonies were only requested from those
who had participated in the first night's events. Presumably, as
Halt was directly involved in the second incident, he considered
there was no need to document those proceedings, plus he had the
verbal notes from his microcassette recording.

Halt confirmed to Sally Rayl, "Around New Year's Eve, I took
statements and interviewed the men who had taken part in the
initial incident".

These were the statements I acquired in 1998 and the existence of
copies was first revealed in 'Rendlesham Unravelled' - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/rendlshm.htm


As four of the five statements record the date of our initial
'UFO' scare and verify it as 26 December, there should never have
been any confusion.

If, as Halt stated in response to my question, he attempted to
substantiate the correct dates before sending his memo, why not
refer to these testimonies he had personally obtained from the
witnesses?


Halt informed the Ministry that following a sighting of "unusual
lights outside the back gate at RAF Woodbridge" a patrol was
permitted to investigate, even though the forest was outwith USAF
jurisdictions. He wrote:

"Thinking an aircraft might have crashed or been forced down,
they called for permission to go outside the gate to investigate.
The on-duty flight chief responded and allowed three patrolmen to
proceed on foot. The individuals reported seeing a strange
glowing object in the forest".

It seems the 'strange glowing object' reported by them turned out
to be a farmhouse, as confirmed in the statement of one
participant, Airman Ed Cabansag:
"We figured the lights were coming from past the forest, since
nothing was visible as we passed through the woody forest. We
could see a glowing near the beacon light, but as we got closer
we found it to be a lit-up farmhouse. After we had passed through
the forest, we thought it had to be an aircraft accident. So did
CSC as well. But we ran and walked a good 2 miles past our
vehicle, until we got to a vantage point where we could determine
that what we were chasing was only a beacon light off in the
distance. Our route through the forest and field was a direct
one, straight towards the light".


Indeed, it was the same 'glowing farmhouse', at Capel Green,
which so alarmed Halt during the second 'UFO' incident, when he
ventured into Rendlesham forest in search of the 'UFO' which had
reportedly been seen again. As he recalled in the interview with
Salley Rayl:

"Just prior to that, we had also noticed that the farmer's house
appeared to be glowing, as though there were a fire inside. All
the windows were bright red and sort of flickering and I was
quite concerned for the occupants of the house".

During the past year, local researcher Robert McLean has on more
than one occasion followed the route documented on Halt's
microcassette recording and, easily locating the same farmhouse,
was able to see for himself the "house on fire effect", which is,
"quite an effective illusion".

It's only a result of local lighting conditions.


Halt's memo continues:

"The object was described as being metallic in appearance and
triangular in shape, approximately two to three meters across the
base and approximately two meters high. It illuminated the entire
forest with a white light. The object itself had a pulsing red
light on top and a bank(s) of blue lights underneath. The object
was hovering or on legs. As the patrolmen approached the object,
it maneuvered through the trees and disappeared. At this time the
animals on a nearby farm went into a frenzy.

The object was briefly sighted approximately an hour later near
the back gate".


Not one of the three Security Police depicted a 'triangular-
shaped' object in their statements. Staff-Sergeant Jim Penniston
was the only participant who claimed to have seen what he
believed to be a metallic object, associated with the 'lights'.
His original written account describes how he was never able to
get closer than 50 meters to the illusive source, which his
accompanying sketch clearly showed to be 'box-shaped' - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/penn6.gif

This story was to changed radically, especially after Penniston
underwent 'regressive hypnosis'. Contrary to his initial
testimony, at some point, the 'object' did then become
'triangular-shaped'.

However, the final member of that patrol, Airman First Class John
Burroughs, was adamant they never observed a 'craft', merely some
lights which implied an object was there. On 20 September, 1991,
Jim Speiser published on ParaNet the transcript of a brief series
of questions which Burroughs had answered. Amongst these was the
following dialogue concerning the 'Unsolved Mysteries'
documentary, broadcast on 18 September:

POWELL: Regarding one of the last clips shown, which depicted one
or two airmen prone as a very nearby and clearly craft-like
object rose from a landing position and took off, do you know if
there were any ground traces of this?

BURROUGHS: First of all, we did not see a structured 'craft' as
was depicted. All we saw were lights that seemed to imply a
structure of some kind. Later inspection showed three round
depressions at that spot, forming an equilateral triangle. The
British Police explained these as 'rabbit holes'.

During a 1993 interview for 'Fate' magazine [Fate 46, No 9,
September 1993, pp 70-71], Burroughs also told Antonio Huneeus,
"I never saw anything metallic or anything hard".

Cabansag's statement refers only to some unfamiliar lights, the
origin of which was never resolved, except for the "beacon
light".

This is not exactly the overall scenario outlined in Halt's memo.

I know that John Burroughs still maintains how only some
anomalous lights were seen, as I've been in touch with him. In
due course, it's anticipated that the informative, first-hand
account which Burroughs has confided will be published.


Neither did the lights 'manoeuvre through the trees and
disappear' as portrayed. Ultimately, the lights were seen next to
a farmhouse, before being lost from sight, as explained in
Burroughs' statement:

"We got up to a fence that separated the trees from the open
field and you could see the lights down by a farmers house. We
climbed over the fence and started heading towards the red and
blue lights and they just disappeared. Once we reached the
farmer's house we could see a beacon going around so we went
towards it. We followed it for about 2 miles before we could see
it was coming from a lighthouse.

We had just crossed a creek and were told to come back when we
saw a blue light to our left in the trees. It was only there for
a min and it just streaked away. After that, we didn't see
anything so we returned to the truck".


Conspicuously absent in Halt's memo is the story of how
Orfordness lighthouse played a role in those first and formative
'UFO' perceptions.

That 'blue light' which seemed to 'streak away' is the sole basis
for Halt's contention, "The object was briefly sighted
approximately an hour later near the back gate".

There was never any 'object' observed again.

And so it goes...

If the Ministry had also been advised by Halt that the tiny,
(confirmed by Halt to Sally Rayl), pulsating light he personally
observed within Rendlesham forest, as further detailed in the
memo, was seen again "clear off to the coast" (documented in his
microcassette recording), the entire context of these 'UFO'
alarms might have become more evident.


One additional factor which Halt drew attention to was 'radiation
readings', taken at what was considered to be the first night's
'UFO landing site'. We can see from the MoD's file that they also
wasted time on this.

It's long been demonstrated that the readings were minuscule -
see for example:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/newslet1.htm

The bottom line is, as detailed therein, is that incidental
'radiation readings' taken from a nearby farmer's field were
actually higher than most of the 'landing site' readings!
It's welcome that the MoD have finally released copies of the
various correspondence which Halt's memo generated and it's a
telling insight.

If the Ministry had realised what was contained within the
original witness statements, it's questionable if they would even
have bothered investigating whether radar tracking evidence
existed.

Although there have been claims a 'UFO' was tracked on radar,
prior to the first incident, it was documented that the radar
tower were contacted and could offer no assistance.

Halt also requested a statement from Flight Controller Fred
Buran, who was stationed at RAF Bentwaters Central Security
Control and had directed operations.

He testified:

"I monitored their progress (Burroughs, Cabansag and Penniston)
as they entered the wooded area".

"Due to the colors they had reported, I alerted them to the fact
that they may have been approaching a light aircraft crash scene.
I directed SSgt Coffey to check with the tower to see if they
could throw some light on the subject. They could not help".


What's unveiled by the MoD's own internal documents could not be
much further removed from a 'cover up'.

It merely serves to once more evidence the extraordinary
misperceptions and fallacious claims which have been inherent to
the 'Rendlesham forest UFOs' and that when further unravelled,
the facts reveal infinitely more about human nature, than not
telling the people ET was here.


Also now set in context are previous comments by Nick Pope, who
worked for the MoD. In order to clarify Pope's exact duties, I
queried this with the Ministry and on 29 September 1999, Gaynor
South, from 'Secretariat(Air Staff)2a' replied:

"Mr Pope was employed as an Executive Officer in Secretariat (Air
Staff) 2. His post was designated Sec(AS)2a.

The main duties of the post concern non-operational RAF
activities overseas and diplomatic clearance policy for military
flights abroad.

A small percentage of time is spent dealing with reports from the
public about alleged 'UFO' sightings and associated public
correspondence".

On 5 May, 1996, Pope was interviewed by 'UFO Magazine' [UK] and
spoke about the Ministry's 'Rendlesham' file, or to be more
precise, its absence:

UFO: In 1980 one of the most extraordinary incidents involving a
UFO occurred in Suffolk, just a few hundred yards from the joint
USAF/RAF bases at Bentwaters and Woodbridge. DS8 was the name of
the MoD's UFO department at that time who handled the case. Your
thoughts on this one?

POPE: Rendlesham is the 'Holy Grail' of British Ufology isn't it?

UFO: It was bigger than DS8 could handle - isn't that true?

POPE: I believe Rendlesham has an extraterrestrial explanation. I
am convinced on the first night of the activity a small remote
craft was seen by the guard patrol. As we all know, trace
evidence was found. Colonel Halt wrote his memorandum to
Whitehall...

UFO: On this insistence of a British officer?

POPE: Yes, but on each joint USAF/RAF base there is an RAF
Commander; but it's really only a nominal title; these facilities
are basically USAF bases. I believe for legal reasons they must
have an RAF Commander who acts as the conduit between the USAF
and the Ministry of Defence. My best assessment of what happened
next is - absolutely nothing! The report was written on the 13th
January and when it arrived at Whitehall, whoever was doing the
job didn't have the faintest idea what to do with it, probably
took one look at it and said, what am I supposed to do? I am
afraid to say it simply ended up in a file.
[END OF EXTRACT]


I'm sure Nick Pope will be interested to see the file which Dr
Clarke and others are now familiar with!

The interview continued:

POPE: The standard line on Rendlesham Forest is that the incident
was looked into, and nothing of defence significance was
uncovered. The challenge, as it where, to the department, is that
we have never seen the analysis.
UFO: But people want to know: who did this analysis? And on what
basis did it conclude there was no threat?

POPE: These are questions you might want to pose to Sec(AS)2a!

UFO: Does this not indicate that DS8 wasn't even a minor player
in the events that followed next. Bentwaters was on full alert
anyway due to the problems in Europe?

POPE: I believe we had just had the situation in Poland with the
trade union Solidarity, and this heightened international
tension.

[...]

UFO: Would it not have been different given such an incident had
occurred whilst you headed Sec(AS)2a? Would you have launched an
investigation?

POPE: I would have been on the first bloody train to Bentwaters!

UFO: What kind of support would you have given?

POPE: I would have taken soil samples, and taken those to the
Defence Radiological Protection Service. I would have immediately
impounded the radar tapes and had them sent to me, and
immediately called RAF defence experts in, we would have sat
down, looked at the tapes and analysed the content to see if they
showed structured craft or spurious returns. Interview statements
would have followed...

UFO: But this allegedly did not happen in 1980?

POPE: At the end of the day this did not happen, so far as I am
aware.

UFO: Perhaps DS8 did these things and there was a general clamp
down of information?

POPE: If that had been the case it would have inevitably leaked
out.
[END OF EXTRACT]


Pope concluded:

UFO: Was there a cover-up?

POPE: No. Not in the MoD - I think the MoD's response was just
ineffective.

UFO: That's a very big statement?

POPE: Yes, but if something of that magnitude was reported and
simply placed on file, then what else can you say?
[END OF EXTRACT]

Contrary to Nick's conjecture that Col Halt's memo "simply ended

"You have questioned whether the Ministry of Defence thoroughly

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Wed, 22 Aug 2001 12:52:15 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] The first abduction

The first abduction I know of in the US is the Betty and Barney Hill
case in New Hampshire on 9/19/1961. It was revealed by hypnosis.

John Fuller's book "The Interrupted Journey" has the transcripts
of the hypnosis sessions.

Of course, since this was the first such case, the hypnotist did not
know that it was possible for his own actions and questions to edit
the event in the minds of the witnesses. There are several places in
the transcript where the hypnotist asked leading questions, and
that can cause the witness to make up details to please the
hypnotist.

The description of the visible object recalled by the witnesses before
the hypnotic sessions is consistent with a night advertizing plane.

Chris wrote:

>In 1767 a strange object was seen in Scotland. The exact source
>is unknown to me...

[...]

>I leave it to your judgment and experience to decide its merits
>as a UFO sighting. Extract of a letter from Edinburgh, Sept. 8,
>1767 follows:
>
>"We hear from Perthsire, that an uncommon phaenomenon was
>observed on the water of Isla, near Cupor Angus, preceded by a
>thick dark smoke, which soon dispelled, and discovered a large
>luminous body, like a house on fire, but presently after took a
>form something pyramidal, and rolled forwards with impetuosity
>till it came to the water of Erick, up which river it took its
>direction, with great rapidity, and disappeared a little above

Chris,

There's a helpful on-line map which sets the claims in context -
see:

http://uk8.multimap.com/map/browse.cgi?scale=200000&X=310000&Y=74
0000&gride=&gridn=&width=700&height=400&client=M6&db=hcgaz&overvi
ewmap=&coordsys=gb&right.x=12&right.y=21

This should of course be entered as a one-line URL.

The river winding just above Coupar is the Isla and north-east we
can see where it meets the Ericht.

Your source refers to the town of Cupor and the river Erick.

As you may know, I live in Scotland and I can't locate any
evidence that Coupar was known as Cupor in 1767 or earlier,
however, according to 'The Gazetteer of Scotland' by W. Chalmers,
published in nearby Dundee during 1803:

"Coupar of Angus or Cupar is a considerable town and parish in
the valley of Strathmore, and though designated in Angus, by far
the greater part is situated in the county of Perth. The town is
situated on the Isla, and is divided by a rivulet into two parts;
that part which lies south of that rivulet being all that belongs
to the county of Angus".

I wonder if 'Cupor' is a typo, during various translations, and
should perhaps be 'Cupar'?


If the 'phaenomenon' [apparently a spelling used in that era]
originated on the river Isla "and rolled forwards with
impetuosity till it came to the water of Erick, up which river it
took its direction, with great rapidity", we seem to have an
unusual occurrence, whatever the explanation.

However, if said artefact "disappeared a little above
Blairgowrie" - which would be about 3 miles or so distant - it's
evidently impossible that the same observer could have witnessed
this.

Isn't our anecdote therefore a collection of different accounts?

As it's allegedly a Scottish chronicle, I would be interested to
pursue any related records and I'll make due enquiries. There
should be a local historical society who can provide assistance.

"In its passage, it carried a large cart many yards over a field
of grass; a man riding along the high road was carried from his
horse, and so stunned with the fall, as to remain senseless a
considerable time. It destroyed one half of a house, and left the
other behind, undermined and destroyed an arch of the new bridge
building at Blairgowrie, immediately after which it disappeared".

If the source was indeed "a form something pyramidal", could this
[presuming it actually happened at all!] have been a 'whirlwind'
or small tornado?

Although thankfully rare in the UK, they do occur - see:

http://www.torro.org.uk/


One prospect for 'hard evidence' is the claim that "an arch of
the new bridge building at Blairgowrie" had been destroyed.

Given that constructing a bridge in 1767 was a notable and
arduous undertaking, we might reasonably assume any sudden
destruction of such endeavours would result in a documented
account somewhere.

If the report has any basis in fact, then it's surely possible to
identify which 'Blairgowrie' bridge was [half] built circa 1767.

Intriguing if there was a contemporary construction - does it
exhibit any evidence which indicates the 'legend' is true?

The original story is perhaps worth following up and let's see
where that leads.


James Easton.

www.ufoworld.co.uk

From: "Luis R. González Manso" <lrgm@arrakis.es>
Date: Thu, 23 Aug 2001 09:39:53 +0200
Subject: [UFORL] The first abduction (LONG)

According to Bullard ("The Measure of a Mystery") the first abduction took
place in 1957 in Austria, but was reported in Canada. Peter Rogerson in
MAGONIA 46 gave more data:

"This story first appeared in the obscurity of the 11 december 1957 issue of
the Prince George Citizen (British Columbia), subsequently in Ralph
Sandbach's "Ufology News" and the May 1958 edition of Ray Palmer's "Flying
Saucers". It was a poorly crafted story in which an American serviceman in
Salzburg was captured by a bug-eyed monster and taken on a trip to Mars on
board a flyinf saucer. The alien was described as being smaller than the
witness, with a high _cylindrical_ forehead, large eyes _with smaller eyes
in them like an insect's_, two holes for a nose, a slit mouth, holes for
ears and a white skull; the torso was round like a tin can. It had no neck,
proportionate legs but short arms which terminated in three-fingered hands.
The story contained one major error, that the narrator and his captor
flipped over as they reached the zone of gravitational neutrality between
the earth and the moon (...)

What is more significant, however, is that this was the first abduction to
be published in a book which circulated beyond the narrow world of ufology.
This was W. Gordon Allen's "Spacecrafts from beyond Three Dimensions",
published in 1959. Now one must concede that it was a turgid work of
pseudoscience, not your first choice for a riveting head, but UFO books were
in short supply in, say, 1962 and this book was in bookshops and libraries
(...) Even if Bettyr Hill hadn't encountered it in her library haul, Allen's
pseudoscientific speculations about ether and the "vortex theory of atoms",
and Nicholas Tesla, were, it strikes me, PRECISELY the sort of thins to
appeal to two of the original investigators of the Hill case, Robert Hohmann
and C.D. Jackson, who were responsible for suggesting to the Hills that they
had experienced "missing time". Even more interesting is that Allen, in this
better-publicised version, edited out references to the cylindrical forehead
and the bug eyes; instead he described the abductor as having "a high
forehead, big eyes, a slit for a mounth, two holes for a nose, white skin,
large skull, no external skin aroun his earhole openings" -much closer to
the Grey, isn't it?"

Any comments?

I would like to judge by myself, so can any of you supply me with copies of
the initial report or the Allen's version?

Continuing the search up to 1973, in David Webb's "1973-Year of the
Humanoids", he mentions only 6 cases:

13C October 1973       Columbus     (conf.) Has there been any report on
this case?
17     11 Oct 1973       Pascagoula
20B 16 Oct 1973          Lehi (Patty Price/Roach) Doubtful (Randles'
abd. book)
24     17 Oct 1973      nr Loxley
37A 25 Oct 1973         Buena Park (B. Scott). Hoax (according to
Lawson)
39     28 Oct 1973       Bahia Blanca (Llanca) Hoax (according to
Banchs and CIU)

Pascagoula is a very strange case that, at least, do not conform to the
standard version. Cases 13C, 20B and 37A were known later directly by
investigators, so it seems that the only other US abduction case divulged at
the time in the media was the case of Clarence Patterson. Is that correct?

Llanca's case reached all around Latin countries (they even mentioned it in
my local paper in a town in Spain) but I do not know if it was mentioned in
the USA at the time.

Clarence Patterson and his pickup truck were sucked up into a huge,
cigar-shaped object with a green light. He was pulled out of the truck by
about six robot-like beings who seemed to read his mind. The next thing he
remenbered, he was back on the highway going about 90 mph in the truck. He
may have been on board for up to 30 minutes. A sulphury smell was noted
during the sighting. First hand investigation.
Has there been any report on this case? I seem to remenber a cover
ilustration in a CUFOS investigator newsletter....

Thanks in advence,

Luis R. González.

Dear James,

Thank you for pointing out the confusion in names. I
shall have to check it in FSR after all, unless Mr.
Rimmer can look it up for us once again...:)

As far as spelling is concerned, nothing would
surprise me from that period.

As for the nature of the phenomenon, I've been
collecting 17th, 18th and 19th C. reports of
pyramid-shaped UFOs for some time. Many of them were
apparently stationary in the sky for up to 3 hours at
a time. Although some have been natural phenomena (and
perhaps all of them, who can tell?), I'll need to
compile more cases before I can reach a personal
conclusion. It was a good time for UFO-spotting in
general (if the term 'UFO' can be applied to
cylinders, spheres, discs, strange rising things and
whacky leaping things without prejudice).

If you can find the original source it would be a
fantastic help, as it's one of those curious incidents
that will emerge again and again and needs to be
reassessed.

Chris

From: chris aubeck <caubeck@yahoo.com>
Date: Fri, 24 Aug 2001 12:15:42 +0100 (BST)
Subject: Re: [UFORL] The first abduction (LONG)


Hello Luis,

The only comment I would make is that you should
choose define your objectives a little more carefully.

The other day you mentioned the earliest French case
(1921). This was published in (excuse me if my memory
does not serve me right here) October 1954 in 'Paris
Match,' which makes it the earliest reported
abduction, predating Bullard's reference by three
years. Paris Match was widely read.

Depending on what you are intending to do, this French
case either indicates a 1954 origin for abduction
reports, or that an alleged abduction occurred as far
back as 1921.

I can see two problems here:

First, although 1954 was the first instance of an
association between extraterrestrials and abduction,
previous to 1947 identical experiences were reported
but associated with entities that were not necessarily
from other planets. You could say "Well, I can't
include those, that's just folklore and fairies" but
EVEN TODAY typical UFO reports are made by people who
believe they have not seen aliens but angels, demons,
goblins or ghosts. In South America and Africa they
see UFOs but call them spirits. Are you saying these
reports should _not_ be dealt with by ufology despite
the obvious ufological nature of the phenomena
described in them? Where do you draw the line - and
why?

Secondly, if articles such as the one published in
Paris Match in 1954 are accepted as indications of
early abductions, then we have to add to your list
some 100 or more alleged abduction events from the
1910s, 1920s, 1930s and 1940s that only came to light
many decades afterwards. Even Antonio Ribera says he
was abducted in 1930, as you know.

Sorry if you think I'm meddling, but the conclusions
you finally reach will be distorted unless you define
your aims more clearly. And I'd like to see you pen a
useful essay on par with your usual high standards of
research.

Un saludo desde un cybercafé cutre en Moratalaz,

Chris Aubeck

1912 morning. Six year old boy living on farm in contact with "space men".
