From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 11 Oct 2001 18:39:56 +0100
Subject: [UFORL] Secret Rendlesham Documents Revealed

[Posted on behalf of David Clarke and Andy Roberts]

MINISTRY OF DEFENCE RELEASE "TOP SECRET"
RENDLESHAM DOCUMENTS

Five documents relating to the alleged UFO Landing at
RAF Woodbridge in 1980 are no longer a secret following a
landmark decision by the MOD's Director of Information
Exploitation.

In March 2001 the MOD agreed to release the contents
of their file following an application by David Clarke under
the Code of Practice on Access to Government Information.

The decision marks a further breakthrough in our
understanding of the events in Rendlesham Forest.

Five documents were with-held from the response under
exemptions to the code, 2 under Exemption 1 (national
security) and 3 under Exemption 2 (internal discussion and
advice to ministers less than 30 years old).

We immediately lodged an appeal against the decision and
an internal review has now been completed. A senior MOD
official has now released the two documents that were
with-held on the grounds of national security.

The five documents - described by UFO Magazine as
"top secret" - are:

1. A letter from the MOD to RAF Watton (Eastern Radar)
and the SOC station, RAF Neatishead, dated 26 January
1981 requesting a statement on radar observations on 29
December 1980.

2. A reply from the Commanding Officer of RAF Neatshead
to MOD (Ops) GE dated 3 February 1981 describing the
results of checks.

3. An internal minute from an MOD official [Pam Titchmarsh],
to a Minister's Office (John Stanley, Ministry of Defence)
submitting a draft response and an accompanying background
note in respect of a Parliamentary Question tabled by Sir
Patrick Wall MP, answered on 24 October 1983.

4. A duplicate copy of the first page of (3) above.
5. An internal Minute from a MOD official to a Minister's
office, submitting a draft response and accompanying background
material in respect of A letter to the Secretary of State for
Defence, Michael Heseltine MP from David Alton MP, which
had enclosed a letter from one of Mr Alton's Constituents.

The released documents and a copy of the judgement will be
posted on the www.flyingsaucery.com Website.

The documents contain no evidence that a cover-up of a
UFO landing ever existed.

We can reveal that the two documents with-held on the
grounds of "national security" do not constitute a 'smoking gun'
- they simply illustrate how claims of a cover-up arise from
secrecy for the sake of secrecy, part of an established tradition
in Britain.

What they reveal is that the RAF were making checks on radar
records for 29 December 1980, following information supplied
by Lt Col Charles Halt in his memo to the MOD.

As we now know the actual date of Halt's sighting in Rendlesham
Forest was the night of 27/28 December 1980. This implies
incompetence and complacency on behalf of the MOD, who
did not see fit to make further inquiries into the details they had
been supplied by Halt.

The correct date was subsequently confirmed by the former
Commanding Officer of RAF Watton who has described his role
in an exclusive interview in June 2001 before any other UFOlogist
was even aware of the MOD file release.

The retired Squadron Leader told us: "I recall the incident well [as]
I was on duty at the time it occurred. I can confirm that the call came
from Bentwaters RAPcom. They requested that we scan the radars
for any radar targets in their area; there were NONE. They
reported flashing lights in the Rendlesham Forest area, outside the
airfield runway [and that] the base police were investigating the
incident."

The officer was on duty on the same night as a civilian radar
operator Nigel Kerr who claims he saw a "blip" on his screen
above the base runway coincident with the report from
Bentwaters. The blip disappeared after several sweeps of the
radar. Kerr's CO dismisses this claim, saying that no such
observation was reported to his Controller at the time, who
oversaw the ATC screens at the joint military/civilian facility.
This is a fact confirmed by the CO in contemporary note in
the MOD file, dated 26 February 1981 that reads:

>"On the night of the reported sighting
>our controller on duty was requested to view the radar;
>nothing was observed. The facts are recorded in our log
>book of that night."

He added that the T84 analogue radars at Watton frequently
detected spurious echoes that behaved exactly as Kerr
described. The lack of radar corroboration was confirmed by
Halt in a 1997 interview when he said:

>"[I] called the command post, asked them to call
>Eastern Radar, responsible for air defence of the
>sector..twice they reported that they didn't see
>anything.."

The Watton CO also confirmed that he personally ordered t
hat all radar tapes - both from 27/28 December and
surrounding dates - should be impounded for examination.
This was not unusual but entirely consistent with MOD
procedure following reports of unusual sightings. In January,
1981 the evidence was removed by a joint RAF/USAF
team from the Military Air Traffic Organisation (MATO)
who apparently found some of the tapes were faulty.

This appears to be the basis of the rumour that USAF
intelligence officers "confiscated" radar tapes from Watton
shortly after the sightings. The CO's evidence can finally
lay this myth to rest.

Claims have been made that the release of the MOD file
is entirely as a result of pressure placed upon the Ministry
by Lord Hill-Norton and Georgina Bruni. Credit is due to
both, but this claim is not correct.

The facts are that during the summer of 2000 the MOD invited
us to submit specific requests for UFO case files under the
terms of the Code of Practice. The Rendlesham File was just
one of a number of files closed under the 30 year rule that
were subsequently requested and released; their contents
will be revealed in our book, "Out of the Shadows: The
British Establishment, UFOs and the Cold War", published
early next year.

My request for the Rendlesham File was submitted in
February 2001 and on 22 March an MOD official wrote
as follows:

"[as a result of your request]. there are a number of
papers that were generated between 1981 and 1983
and later assembled on one file, along with correspondence
received after 1983 from members of the public.Briefings
to Ministers in respect of PQs asked on the subject since
1983 are placed on another File. On the file containing
papers on the alleged incident in Rendlesham Forest,
there is an internalminute that appears to summarise the
extent of MOD investigation and draws the conclusion
that has been used in all subsequent briefings.

"We are content to photocopy the documents from that file,
which consists of somewhere in the region of 70 enclosures.
This, along with some sanitising and review will be undertaken
free of charge following your application under the Code of
Practice."

This proves that our application was made and processed
following MOD procedure that was entirely independent
of Lord Hill-Norton who received the file some time after
we did.

We wish to pay tribute to all those who have contributed to
the research into the Rendlesham case, regardless of their
opinions and personal approach to the subject. That includes
Georgina Bruni, Jenny Randles, James Easton, Ian Ridapth,
Nick Redfern and others who have all contributed to our
knowledge of the Rendlesham forest mystery in their
own way.

Keep watching www.flyingsaucery.com for further revelations.

Happy trails,

David Clarke and Andy Roberts

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Tue, 16 Oct 2001 00:49:08 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Rendlesham: Radiation Readings

Regarding Tim and Rob's comments - I've never seen the AN/PDR-27
user manual advertised and it would interesting to obtain even a
photocopy.

Some further information concerning the AN/PDR-27, obtained from
various sources:

The AN/PDR-27 is used as a point source instrument to monitor low
levels of radiation contamination on personnel, supplies, and
equipment.

It is used to detect BETA radiation and measures and detect gamma
radiation.

The AN/PDR-27 is a Beta-Gamma radiation survey meter, with end
window density 1.5mg/cm2 [squared], range 0.01mR/hr to 500mR/hr,
two or more per facility.

The AN/PDR-27 is capable of detecting beta and gamma radiation
simultaneously when the beta shield is removed.

The scales are provided on the AN/PDR-27 RADIAC are:

1. 0-500 milliroentgens
2. 0-50 milliroentgens
3. 0-5 milliroentgens
4. 0-.5 milliroengens


[By comparison, scales on the AN/PDR-43 RADIAC are:

1. 0-500 Roentgens
2. 0-50 Roentgens
3. 0-5 Roentgens

There is no 'point five', lower scale].


AN/PDR-27 detects GAMMA on all scales and BETA on the two lower
scales when the BETA shield has been opened.

The operator is instructed to "Hold the probe within 1 inch of
the object being monitored".
[END]
There's some further, related background material I've yet to
publish [Tim might be amused that another former AN/PDR-27
operator says it was a 'piece of shit'!] and I'll summarise all
of this in due course.

Some interesting feedback has come from Joe McGonagle on the
UpDates list - see:

http://www.ufomind.com/ufo/updates/2001/oct/m10-006.shtml
http://www.ufomind.com/ufo/updates/2001/oct/m12-010.shtml

I've replied to that with, hopefully, further insight into the
readings taken. A major factor which now emerges is how many of
the readings were clearly taken with the probe in 'mid-air'.


Any responses to Joe's remarks are welcome.


James Easton.

From: "Robert McLean" <robert.mclean2@virgin.net>
Date: Thu, 18 Oct 2001 02:26:54 +0100
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Who bought Bentwaters?

This is all a bit off topic, but since you ask . . .

As far as I am aware, Bentwaters was never sold to a Middle Eastern
international investor.

The first potential buyer, The Chris Parker Group, failed to complete a deal
to buy the base from the MoD back in 1996. See
http://www.bentwaters.org.uk/archive/1999.htm

CPG wanted to dig up the runway, and sell it as hardcore.

Then, His Holiness Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and his Natural Law Party nearly
bought the site. I kid you not. Actually, they probably would have made good
owners of the site, as their plan was to turn it into a University, where
students could learn their philosophy/religion, radiate lots of good
vibrations of peace etc, and practice their yogic flying on the 2 mile long
runway.

For reasons that were never made clear, this deal also fell through.
Probably, the MoD was holding out for too much money, as they were
determined to make as much as they could on the sale.

The MoD did sell off the housing, both at RAF Bentwaters and RAF Woodbridge.

The site was eventually bought by Anglia Airparks International. They have
leased some of the buildings, as light industrial units, but most of the
site looks like a ghost town. They also wanted to turn the runway into
serious competition for Stanstead and Norwich airports, and set up a service
centre for aircraft and aeroengines, which would have meant big jets flying
in and out any time of day. The fact that there are no good access roads did
not worry them.

In one direction, the runway points directly at the quiet town of Woodbridge
about 2 miles away, and in the other direction it points directly at the
concert hall at Snape about 3 miles away, where the world famous Aldeburgh
Festival is held every year. Under an informal agreement, the USAF used to
schedule their flying so as not to interrupt performances, but such control
would not be possible with civilian flying. It would have cost £1M to sound
proof the concert hall.

The whole area around Bentwaters is designated an "area of outstanding
natural beauty", and tourism is one of the largest local industries. Most
local polititans supported the Airpark plan, and most local people didn't.
After much local controversy, the plan was eventually killed by a Government
"inspector" in London. Unlike the cold war, there was no over-riding
national interest for re-activating the runway.
Now AIA wants out, and the Chris Parker Group again wants to buy the site,
and dig up the runway. If it goes through it will take about 3 or 4 years to
truck it out. Sod's Law being what it is, we'll probably be in another cold
war with a different enemy by then, and the Government will wish the runway
was still there.

At least RAF Woodbridge has been maintained, even though it's in mothballs.

Best regards

Robert McLean

-----Original Message-----
From: Tony Eccles <tonyeccles@yahoo.com>Date: 19 October 2001 11:27
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?


>Steve,
>this hasn't been exactly true for aircraft leaving

Hi,

Gliding civilian aircraft are a fact - or were and I bet still are in
places.

The story is told in 'The UFOs that Never Were' but briefly.

In the Rossendale Valley (25 miles north of Manchester) we were getting a
flood of reports of an orange light moving silently through the sky,
swooping on farmers and climbing away into cloud. We (at the local UFO
group) had so many scared witnesses - including police officers - that we
knew this was a real phenomenon as it was too consistent. They all said it
could not be aircraft as there were no flashing lights - just the single
orange/red glow.

We soon realised there was a pattern. The sightings all occurred at around 2
am. They were all heading in the same direction (north to south). And often
on the same day of the week. So we set a trap.

We had teams of skywatchers on the hills to track the object on the next
likely night. One of our team was also allowed to man the radar at
Manchester International Airport logging all incoming traffic.

We saw the UFO, tracked it on radar and proved what it was. It was a cargo
plane operated by a major carrier (still flying today) who were breaking CAA
rules. They were - on fine nights - throttling back the engine, switching
off all cabin lights and nav lights and only leaving on their tail fin
illumination. The carriers logo was red. Hence the floating glow! The crew
throttled back up as they crossed Rossendale and now saw the lights of the
northern fringes of Greater Manchester below. They did not realise they were
being seen from below assuming they were over open moor (as they mostly
were) - but reckoned without terrified farmers and coppers!

Manchester accepted this answer, censured the crew and said they knew that
gliding did sometimes occur. But it was frowned upon. I bet it still happens
though.

Those in the UK or any country that screens the long running ITV series
'Heartbeat' might recognise the above. They actually took our MUFORA group
investigation and turned it into an episode of the drama series (about rural
police on the Yorkshire Moors in the l960s) - in which, naturally, it was
not a UFOlogist but a brilliant retired policeman that solved the case. But
otherwise they changed nothing of the actual facts - the culprit plane
still being a cargo flight from Scotland (as indeed it was in reality).

MUFORA got no credit for this story line BTW. I did ask the producer why
ot - since it was so blatantly ripped off from our work - but got no
answer. But the incredulous looks on the police officers faces on TV when
their ex colleague revealed the truth about a gliding cargo plane to them
was a picture - made all the more amusing for us in MUFORA in that we knew
exactly how they felt and probably wouldnt have believed this either in
real life if we had not cracked this case by actual investigation.

The above real events were in the late 1970s / early l980s (the TV episode
was made in l997) - so I dont know if this has been entirely eliminated but
my guess is that over very rural areas some crew will still be putting their
feet up, watching the sky and gliding whilst enjoying the view on nice
nights - just as were the crew of Air Cargo 101 (as I have always called
this airline's flight in order to prevent us getting sued by a major airline
for exposing this dubious practice!)

Best wishes,

Jenny Randles

Gianni Lucarini, "Gli extraterrestri esistono", Mediterranee, Roma 1974. I
have it here in front of me. The author was a member of Italian contactee
group "Contact International Italia" and did write two bad books on the
subject. In that book he had a chronology of sightings since the Tulli
papyrus (again!) to 1949 (don't ask, I'm going to photocopy that all for
you). There it is, indeed.

>vi) According to the Spanish article, Lucarini’s
>source was the Italian publication “La aviación de
>otros planetas.”

True: "L'aviazione di altri pianeti", january 1968 issue. It was the
mimeographed bulletin of CISAER (Centro Italiano Studi Aviazione
Elettromagnetica Roma), the group founded by Italian diplomate and pioneer
ufologist Alberto Perego (the same man who had dozens of sightings, the
most famous being that flock of birds --- err! Ufos --- in a cross
formation above the Vatican in November, 1954). As of 1968 I seem to
remember it was edited by his secretary, Mr. Giuseppe Lazzari, who soon
changed its name to "Cielo e terra". As we obviously own a complete
collection (1958-1976), I'll trace it back soon for you: it sounds like a
chronology of old centuries sightings (as Lucarini gives it as a source for
many a reports in that chapter), so it might result like a new source of
sources for you, on turn.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>

Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

That means these aircraft are flying illegally and should be reported! It is
possible, of course, that people simply don't see all the lights. Even
though I know what lights an aircraft shows at night, and have night-flying
experience, I am still occasionally taken aback when I see a light in the
sky that doesn't seem to conform to the standard pattern. I watch carefully
and eventually can resolve the individual lights. This is all down to
relative position and atmospheric effects. Plus, of course, distance is
impossible to judge at night, and those lights carry much further than you'd
think. On my first night training flight - a cross-country in Florida - I
was amazed that I was easily picking out aircraft that must have been 20
miles away or more. Until, that was, the Shuttle launched (some 70 miles
from our position) and everything turned to day! (Still logged it as night
though...)

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Mon, 22 Oct 2001 09:02:58 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

It seems rather large in angular size for one aircraft. Two, maybe....

Some airliners and military vehicles have all red navigation lights, an
indication that all other planes are to give way to them.

I was thinking of a prank where people tie railroad or highway flares
to helium balloons, or build hot air balloons with suit bags and
candles. The wind then carries them along. The following surprising
facts emerge from investigations where this identity was confirmed:

1. The balloons were a are a lot closer than the witness thought.

2. The witness size estimate was always at least 10 times larger
than the actual size of the object (lighted area about 1.5 feet in
diameter max - usually the balloon bag above is invisible, but it is
rarely larger than 4 feet in the longest dimension).

3. The speed estimate was always much higher than the real speed.

4. The altitude estimate was always much higher than the real
altitude.

My research indicates that these errors are due to two factors, the
inability of the human visual system to determine distance under
these circumstances, and the proclivity of the human sensory
system to use the first guess of what the object might be to arrive at
values for the size, distance, altitude, and speed.

If an unknown light or object is seen against the night sky, there is
no way anyone can tell how far away it is if it is farther away than
30 feet.

*****

One of my favorite examples of a fire-balloon case happened in
Jefferson County, Kentucky on February 26, 1993:

Witnesses on the ground reported a strange light in the sky.

A police helicopter responded to the call, and found the light.

The policemen in the helicopter reported that the UFO was larger than
the helicopter, and kept making ramming passes at the helicopter.

The people on the ground reported that the nearly stationary light
was much smaller than the helicopter, and that the helicopter kept
passing the object, as though it could not find it.

Both groups reported the object suddenly dived and went out.

When the sighting made the papers, the amateur weatherman who
released the balloon came forward and told authorities what it was.

*****

In another case in 1965 (I don't have the exact date or location), a
fire balloon appeared to "outrun" a jet fighter - but only from the
vantage point of the group of witnesses. The very slow and close
fire balloon just happened to be blown by the wind in such a way
that it stayed "ahead" of the unrelated jet which was much farther
away. A witness in another location would not have seen the UFO
to be anywhere near the jet, but in an entirely different part of the
sky.

*****

Like I said, the unaided human visual system can't ever make the
kind of measurements needed - even seasoned pilots can't do it.

Now if the observer knows what the object is, that's different - he has
its true size in his memory, and all of the other values fall into place
nicely.

@ Chris

This is the same mistake most observers of fire balloons make.

They grossly overestimate the speed because they overestimate the
distance and size of the balloon -- usually by at least a factor of 10,
most times by a factor of 50 or more. It happens again and again and
again in cases where the balloon was later positively identified. Usually
the cause of this mistake is the assumption by the witness that the
UFO is a vehicle capable of carrying men, combined with the inherent
limitations of human vision.

If both balloons are in the same wind, they will both do the same
thing in parallel. Only when turbulence occurs in the wind will they do
different things.

Until people realize that the human visual system is totally incapable
of measuring the distance to an UNKNOWN object more than 30 feet
away without aid, the serious study of UFOs will never progress
beyond that of the 'bloids.

Larry

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Mon, 22 Oct 2001 21:10:52 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

Can you supply a source or reference to this 'all-red navigation lights'
business? It sounds complete nonsense and I've certainly never come across
any such thing in the Air Navigation Order.

It doesn't make much sense. The whole point of the design of navigation
lights is that they tell you which way an aircraft is flying, to help you
determine if there is a risk of collision. The lights have deliberately, and
legally mandated, restricted angles of view (110 degrees for the wingtip
lights, 140 degrees for the rear). For example, if you can see one red and
one white light, you know that you are looking at the port side of the
aircraft, but that it is moving away from you (ie, you are in the aircraft's
rear-left quarter). If you can see both red and green lights, the aircraft
is coming at you. You would never see all three lights unless directly above
or below the aircraft. It's quite common to see just one nav light - plus
other lights such as high-intensity, anti-collision strobes, the flashing
red anti-collision beacon (which must flash to differentiate it from the
port nav light), and a tail light. Note, these are the *only* other lights
allowed.

This scheme is needed because the angular velocity of other aircraft is very
small until you are relatively very close.

The three basic nav lights (red, green, white, all steady) are mandatory on
all powered aircraft flying at night. HOWEVER, on some other aircraft, they
are optional. Gliders and free balloons need show only a steady red light.

This 'all-red nav light' thing sounds like a myth or something misunderstood
by a lay person. I'd be interested to know where it's come from.

a+
Steve

It seems rather large in angular size for one aircraft. Two, maybe....

Some airliners and military vehicles have all red navigation lights, an
indication that all other planes are to give way to them.

I was thinking of a prank where people tie railroad or highway flares
to helium balloons, or build hot air balloons with suit bags and
candles. The wind then carries them along. The following surprising
facts emerge from investigations where this identity was confirmed:

1. The balloons were a are a lot closer than the witness thought.

2. The witness size estimate was always at least 10 times larger
than the actual size of the object (lighted area about 1.5 feet in
diameter max - usually the balloon bag above is invisible, but it is
rarely larger than 4 feet in the longest dimension).

3. The speed estimate was always much higher than the real speed.

4. The altitude estimate was always much higher than the real
altitude.

My research indicates that these errors are due to two factors, the
inability of the human visual system to determine distance under
these circumstances, and the proclivity of the human sensory
system to use the first guess of what the object might be to arrive at
values for the size, distance, altitude, and speed.

If an unknown light or object is seen against the night sky, there is
no way anyone can tell how far away it is if it is farther away than
30 feet.

*****

One of my favorite examples of a fire-balloon case happened in
Jefferson County, Kentucky on February 26, 1993:

Witnesses on the ground reported a strange light in the sky.

A police helicopter responded to the call, and found the light.

The policemen in the helicopter reported that the UFO was larger than
the helicopter, and kept making ramming passes at the helicopter.

The people on the ground reported that the nearly stationary light
was much smaller than the helicopter, and that the helicopter kept
passing the object, as though it could not find it.

Both groups reported the object suddenly dived and went out.

When the sighting made the papers, the amateur weatherman who
released the balloon came forward and told authorities what it was.
*****

In another case in 1965 (I don't have the exact date or location), a
fire balloon appeared to "outrun" a jet fighter - but only from the
vantage point of the group of witnesses. The very slow and close
fire balloon just happened to be blown by the wind in such a way
that it stayed "ahead" of the unrelated jet which was much farther
away. A witness in another location would not have seen the UFO
to be anywhere near the jet, but in an entirely different part of the
sky.

*****

Like I said, the unaided human visual system can't ever make the
kind of measurements needed - even seasoned pilots can't do it.

Now if the observer knows what the object is, that's different - he has
its true size in his memory, and all of the other values fall into place
nicely.

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Mon, 22 Oct 2001 23:45:37 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

I have seen them myself.

The colors on a plane, just as the colors on a boat, direct the
approaching plane (or boat) to take appropriate action. If you see
red, you have to pass astern of the other craft. If you see green, the
other craft is to pass astern of you. If you see white, you can pass
on either side. If you see brilliant white, or red AND green, you must
turn to your right (the green side).

Sailboats and rowboats have multiple white lights, or red lights on the
front and white ones on the back, because other boats must give way
to them. Some ocean liners and tankers also have red lights that shine
low, and normal navigation lights that shine high, since small craft have
to give way to them (similar to a car giving way to a train - the weight is
too great for the large ship to take avoiding action in time). I have a
book that shows the various lighting configurations for each class of
vessel and what other classes that vessel must give way to.

Certain military aircraft, slow helicopters, unpowered aircraft, and
some diplomatic planes have all red lights, because other planes
must always give way to them.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Wed, 24 Oct 2001 11:32:22 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

I'm sorry, but this is nonsense.

You're right about the action to take in the case of red and green lights,
because, like boats, aircraft give way to other craft to their right. You're
wrong about white lights. If you see a steady white light on an aircraft,
that means you're looking at its tail. If you overtake, it must be to the
right of the other aircraft. Aircraft can carry only four types of white
light - the steady rear nav light; flashing, high-intensity strobes; landing
lights; and - in the case of airliners - 'logo lights' illuminating the fin.
So, by 'brilliant white' I assume you mean landing lights.

But, while studying air law, I have never seen any reference to military or
diplomatic aircraft carrying only red lights, nor any reference to having to
give way to them. This would be (in the context of why aircraft carry such
lights to start with) rather dangerous. Can you provide the relevant FAR or
ANO reference?

As for seeing them yourself, I suggest you misinterpreted what you saw.

a+
Steve

-----Original Message-----
From: Robinson, Larry [mailto:lrobins@indiana.edu]
Sent: 23 October 2001 06:46Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?


I have seen them myself.

The colors on a plane, just as the colors on a boat, direct the
approaching plane (or boat) to take appropriate action. If you see
red, you have to pass astern of the other craft. If you see green, the
other craft is to pass astern of you. If you see white, you can pass
on either side. If you see brilliant white, or red AND green, you must
turn to your right (the green side).

Sailboats and rowboats have multiple white lights, or red lights on the
front and white ones on the back, because other boats must give way
to them. Some ocean liners and tankers also have red lights that shine
low, and normal navigation lights that shine high, since small craft have
to give way to them (similar to a car giving way to a train - the weight is
too great for the large ship to take avoiding action in time). I have a
book that shows the various lighting configurations for each class of
vessel and what other classes that vessel must give way to.

Certain military aircraft, slow helicopters, unpowered aircraft, and
some diplomatic planes have all red lights, because other planes
must always give way to them.

@ -----Original Message-----
@ From: rotsky [mailto:rotsky@wanadoo.fr]

@
@ Can you supply a source or reference to this 'all-red
@ navigation lights'
@ business? It sounds complete nonsense and I've certainly
@ never come across
@ any such thing in the Air Navigation Order.
@
@ It doesn't make much sense. The whole point of the design of
@ navigation
@ lights is that they tell you which way an aircraft is flying,
@ to help you
@ determine if there is a risk of collision. The lights have
@ deliberately, and
@ legally mandated, restricted angles of view (110 degrees for
@ the wingtip
@ lights, 140 degrees for the rear). For example, if you can
@ see one red and
@ one white light, you know that you are looking at the port side of the
@ aircraft, but that it is moving away from you (ie, you are in
@ the aircraft's
@ rear-left quarter). If you can see both red and green lights,
@ the aircraft
@ is coming at you. You would never see all three lights unless
@ directly above
@ or below the aircraft. It's quite common to see just one nav
@ light - plus
@ other lights such as high-intensity, anti-collision strobes,
@ the flashing
@ red anti-collision beacon (which must flash to differentiate
@ it from the
@ port nav light), and a tail light. Note, these are the *only*
@ other lights
@ allowed.
@
@ This scheme is needed because the angular velocity of other
@ aircraft is very
@ small until you are relatively very close.
@
@ The three basic nav lights (red, green, white, all steady)
@ are mandatory on
@ all powered aircraft flying at night. HOWEVER, on some other
@ aircraft, they
@ are optional. Gliders and free balloons need show only a
@ steady red light.
@
@ This 'all-red nav light' thing sounds like a myth or
@ something misunderstood
@ by a lay person. I'd be interested to know where it's come from.
@

@ to helium balloons, or build hot air balloons with suit bags and
@ candles. The wind then carries them along. The following surprising
@ facts emerge from investigations where this identity was confirmed:
@
@ 1. The balloons were a are a lot closer than the witness thought.
@
@ 2. The witness size estimate was always at least 10 times larger
@ than the actual size of the object (lighted area about 1.5 feet in
@ diameter max - usually the balloon bag above is invisible, but it is
@ rarely larger than 4 feet in the longest dimension).
@
@ 3. The speed estimate was always much higher than the real speed.
@
@ 4. The altitude estimate was always much higher than the real
@ altitude.
@
@ My research indicates that these errors are due to two factors, the
@ inability of the human visual system to determine distance under
@ these circumstances, and the proclivity of the human sensory
@ system to use the first guess of what the object might be to arrive at
@ values for the size, distance, altitude, and speed.
@
@ If an unknown light or object is seen against the night sky, there is
@ no way anyone can tell how far away it is if it is farther away than
@ 30 feet.
@
@ *****
@
@ One of my favorite examples of a fire-balloon case happened in
@ Jefferson County, Kentucky on February 26, 1993:
@
@ Witnesses on the ground reported a strange light in the sky.
@
@ A police helicopter responded to the call, and found the light.
@
@ The policemen in the helicopter reported that the UFO was larger than
@ the helicopter, and kept making ramming passes at the helicopter.
@
@ The people on the ground reported that the nearly stationary light
@ was much smaller than the helicopter, and that the helicopter kept
@ passing the object, as though it could not find it.
@
@ Both groups reported the object suddenly dived and went out.
@
@ When the sighting made the papers, the amateur weatherman who
@ released the balloon came forward and told authorities what it was.
@
@ *****
@
@ In another case in 1965 (I don't have the exact date or location), a
@ fire balloon appeared to "outrun" a jet fighter - but only from the
@ vantage point of the group of witnesses. The very slow and close
@ fire balloon just happened to be blown by the wind in such a way
@ that it stayed "ahead" of the unrelated jet which was much farther
@ away. A witness in another location would not have seen the UFO
@ to be anywhere near the jet, but in an entirely different part of the
@ sky.
@
@ *****
@
@ Like I said, the unaided human visual system can't ever make the
@ kind of measurements needed - even seasoned pilots can't do it.
@
@ Now if the observer knows what the object is, that's
@ different - he has
@ its true size in his memory, and all of the other values fall
@ into place
@ nicely.

@
@ The colors on a plane, just as the colors on a boat, direct the
@ approaching plane (or boat) to take appropriate action. If you see
@ red, you have to pass astern of the other craft. If you see green, the
@ other craft is to pass astern of you. If you see white, you can pass
@ on either side. If you see brilliant white, or red AND green, you must
@ turn to your right (the green side).
@
@ Sailboats and rowboats have multiple white lights, or red
@ lights on the
@ front and white ones on the back, because other boats must give way
@ to them. Some ocean liners and tankers also have red lights that shine
@ low, and normal navigation lights that shine high, since
@ small craft have
@ to give way to them (similar to a car giving way to a train -
@ the weight is
@ too great for the large ship to take avoiding action in
@ time). I have a
@ book that shows the various lighting configurations for each class of
@ vessel and what other classes that vessel must give way to.
@
@ Certain military aircraft, slow helicopters, unpowered aircraft, and
@ some diplomatic planes have all red lights, because other planes
@ must always give way to them.

@@
@ @ Can you supply a source or reference to this 'all-red
@ @ navigation lights'
@ @ business? It sounds complete nonsense and I've certainly
@ @ never come across
@ @ any such thing in the Air Navigation Order.
@@
@ @ It doesn't make much sense. The whole point of the design of
@ @ navigation
@ @ lights is that they tell you which way an aircraft is flying,
@ @ to help you
@ @ determine if there is a risk of collision. The lights have
@ @ deliberately, and
@ @ legally mandated, restricted angles of view (110 degrees for
@ @ the wingtip
@ @ lights, 140 degrees for the rear). For example, if you can
@ @ see one red and
@ @ one white light, you know that you are looking at the port
@ side of the
@ @ aircraft, but that it is moving away from you (ie, you are in
@ @ the aircraft's
@ @ rear-left quarter). If you can see both red and green lights,
@ @ the aircraft
@ @ is coming at you. You would never see all three lights unless
@ @ directly above
@ @ or below the aircraft. It's quite common to see just one nav
@ @ light - plus
@ @ other lights such as high-intensity, anti-collision strobes,
@ @ the flashing
@ @ red anti-collision beacon (which must flash to differentiate
@ @ it from the
@ @ port nav light), and a tail light. Note, these are the *only*
@ @ other lights
@ @ allowed.
@@
@ @ This scheme is needed because the angular velocity of other
@ @ aircraft is very
@ @ small until you are relatively very close.
@@
@ @ The three basic nav lights (red, green, white, all steady)
@ @ are mandatory on
@ @ all powered aircraft flying at night. HOWEVER, on some other
@ @ aircraft, they
@ @ are optional. Gliders and free balloons need show only a
@ @ steady red light.
@@
@ @ This 'all-red nav light' thing sounds like a myth or
@ @ something misunderstood
@ @ by a lay person. I'd be interested to know where it's come from.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Thu, 25 Oct 2001 11:36:00 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

By the way, Larry, the reason I'm so keen to get this issue of nav lights
sorted is that aircraft play such a large role in supposed UFO sightings.
I've lost count of the number of times I've seen ufologists spout so-called
aviation facts (I'm not counting you in this!) to support their claims that
such-and-such 'couldn't have been an aircraft' or 'must have been a top
secret aircraft' and so on. Very often, UFO reports show a lack of
knowledge, lack of understanding or complete misrepresentation of aviation
facts, rules and procedures. They also frequently show no understanding of
the nature of flight, and particularly how it is perceived from the ground
("it couldn't have been an aircraft because there was no noise (it's high or
it's windy), it seemed to stop/suddenly accelerate (it's turned), it was too
slow (it's high, or coming straight at you)..."

So I'm not having a go at you... just want to get this clear. For the
record, here are the Federal Aviation Regulations, FAR 25.1385, FAR 25.1397
and FAR 25.1401, that stipulate lights to be carried and their colour:

§ 25.1385 Position light system installation.
(a) General. Each part of each position light system must meet the
applicable requirements of this section and each system as a whole must meet
the requirements of §§ 25.1387 through 25.1397.
(b) Forward position lights. Forward position lights must consist of a red
and a green light spaced laterally as far apart as practicable and installed
forward on the airplane so that, with the airplane in the normal flying
position, the red light is on the left side and the green light is on the
right side. Each light must be approved.
(c) Rear position light. The rear position light must be a white light
mounted as far aft as practicable on the tail or on each wing tip, and must
be approved.
(d) Light covers and color filters. Each light cover or color filter must be
at least flame resistant and may not change color or shape or lose any
appreciable light transmission during normal use.
[Doc. No. 5066, 29 FR 18291, Dec. 24, 1964, as amended by Amdt. 25-38, 41 FR
55468, Dec. 20, 1976]

§ 25.1397 Color specifications.
Each position light color must have the applicable International Commission
on Illumination chromaticity coordinates as follows:
(a) Aviation red --
"y" is not greater than 0.335; and
"z" is not greater than 0.002.
(b) Aviation green --
"x" is not greater than 0.440-0.320 y ;
"x" is not greater than y -- 0.170; and
"y" is not less than 0.390-0.170 x.
(c) Aviation white --
"x" is not less than 0.300 and not greater than 0.540;
"y" is not less than "x -- 0.040" or "y0 -- 0.010", whichever is the
smaller; and
"y" is not greater than "x+0.020" nor "0.636-0.400 x";
Where "y0" is the "y" coordinate of the Planckian radiator for the value of
"x" considered.
[Doc. No. 5066, 29 FR 18291, Dec. 24, 1964, as amended by Amdt. 25-27, 36 FR
12972, July 10, 1971]

§ 25.1401 Anticollision light system.
(a) General. The airplane must have an anticollision light system that --
(1) Consists of one or more approved anticollision lights located so that
their light will not impair the crew's vision or detract from the
conspicuity of the position lights; and
(2) Meets the requirements of paragraphs (b) through (f) of this section.
(b) Field of coverage. The system must consist of enough lights to
illuminate the vital areas around the airplane considering the physical
configuration and flight characteristics of the airplane. The field of
coverage must extend in each direction within at least 75 degrees above and
75 degrees below the horizontal plane of the airplane, except that a solid
angle or angles of obstructed visibility totaling not more than 0.03
steradians is allowable within a solid angle equal to 0.15 steradians
centered about the longitudinal axis in the rearward direction.
(c) Flashing characteristics. The arrangement of the system, that is, the
number of light sources, beam width, speed of rotation, and other
characteristics, must give an effective flash frequency of not less than 40,
nor more than 100 cycles per minute. The effective flash frequency is the
frequency at which the airplane's complete anticollision light system is
observed from a distance, and applies to each sector of light including any
overlaps that exist when the system consists of more than one light source.
In overlaps, flash frequencies may exceed 100, but not 180 cycles per
minute.
(d) Color. Each anticollision light must be either aviation red or aviation
white and must meet the applicable requirements of § 25.1397.
(e) Light intensity. The minimum light intensities in all vertical planes,
measured with the red filter (if used) and expressed in terms of "effective"
intensities, must meet the requirements of paragraph (f) of this section.
The following relation must be assumed:
[equation graphic missing - can't be easily simulated in ASCII]
where: Ie=effective intensity (candles). I(t)=instantaneous intensity as a
function of time. t2 -- t1=flash time interval (seconds). Normally, the
maximum value of effective intensity is obtained when t2 and t1 are chosen
so that the effective intensity is equal to the instantaneous intensity at
t2 and t1.
(f) Minimum effective intensities for anticollision lights. Each
anticollision light effective intensity must equal or exceed the applicable
values in the following table.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                               Effective
       Angle above or below the horizontal plane                     intensity
                                                      (candles)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
0 deg. to 5 deg.............................................    400
5 deg. to 10 deg............................................     240
10 deg. to 20 deg...........................................      80
20 deg. to 30 deg...........................................      40
30 deg. to 75 deg...........................................      20
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Doc. No. 5066, 29 FR 18291, Dec. 24, 1964, as amended by Amdt. 25-27, 36 FR
12972, July 10, 1971; Amdt. 25-41, 42 FR 36970, July 18, 1977]

<BR>I am not here to debate you or be your Peer.
<BR>
<BR>Any important research should be sound so
<BR>we all get the right data &amp; facts - that's all
<BR>we ask. The propagation of errors just creates
<BR>knock on problems, and in the end trash for the
<BR>rest of us to pick up and correct or live with.
<BR>
<BR>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbs
p;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&n
bsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;---
<BR>
<BR>So, back to my original problem &amp; questions -
<BR>see the next post.
<BR>
<BR>
<BR>My respect to you all,
<BR>
<BR>
<BR>Glen Hough

@ -----Original Message-----
@ From: cgibson@skomer.u-net.com [mailto:cgibson@skomer.u-net.com]
@ Sent: Wednesday, October 24, 2001 14:16
@ To: UFORL@yahoogroups.com
@ Subject: [UFORL] Re: Any ideas?
@
@
@
@ So...these fire balloons were subject to the same wind
@ conditions producing
@ a parallel track.
@
@ 1) the ambient wind conditions were a 7 - 8 knot breeze from the South
@ East. (in fact it was almost flat calm when I was out of the
@ car)

So far, so good.

@ Lights
@ were moving from west to east at a speed in excess of an airliner.

You can NOT know this. You cannot know the actual speed any more
than you can know the actual size or distance, without additional
visual aids.

Your speed estimate is based on your GUESS that it was an aircraft,
which then implied aircraft size and distance values. But if the object
was really a lot smaller and closer, the speed was a lot lower too.

@ 2) Different winds at different levels? Of course. But would
@ a fire balloon
@ be so bright at high altitude (assuming fire balloons can reach such
@ altitudes) and stay alight in such winds. Flimsy bits of kit
@ apparently.
The wind on the ground is usually less than the wind at 50 feet up,
due to the frictional effects of houses, hills, trees, etc.

Fire balloons rarely exceed 1000 feet in altitude.

@ 3) What type of burners do these fire balloons use? What chemicals
@ are added to the fuel to produce a red colour?

The typical burner consists of several candles. At very small angular
sizes at night, the eye sees a more saturated color than what is
actually there. The color of the candle wax can enter into it too,
since it is illuminated by the flame. In my first fire balloon sighting,
one balloon was yellow-orange, and the other was red-orange, both
more saturated than I would expect from a candle.

Try this experiment. Get some candles of various colors, set them
up, and light them. Then walk away until the flames are star sized.
Observe the colors.

A variant uses a helium balloon and a railroad or highway flare.
There, the color is the color of the flare, and the object is much
brighter. In this case, strontium salts produce the red.

@ Still no response to my question about UK fire balloons.

I've been busy. I don't have any recent UK cases. The last confirmed
fire balloon case I have is in Arizona in 1997, seen shortly after the
Phoenix flare drop, on the same night.

North South air route. In an area with 3 major airports within 30 miles,
under a major air route.

I had hoped for better, but fire baloons it is.

Obviously I've been watching the wrong patch of sky for 10 years.

Chris

Your use of Yahoo! Groups is subject to http://docs.yahoo.com/info/terms/
From: Mendoza <Horseman@onetel.net.uk>
Date: Thu, 25 Oct 2001 23:58:09 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?


At 10:36 +0100 25/10/01, rotsky wrote:

>By the way, Larry, the reason I'm so keen
>to get this issue of nav lights sorted is
>that aircraft play such a large role in
>supposed UFO sightings.

[...]

>So I'm not having a go at you... just want to
>get this clear. For the record, here are the
>Federal Aviation Regulations, FAR 25.1385, FAR 25.1397
>and FAR 25.1401, that stipulate lights to be
>carried and their colour:

Hear hear to the first paragraph, but as for the
second... useful, but perhaps not in this case,
which occurred in Leicestershire, England.

No matter what the law may say Joe Public must or
must not do, there are significant exeptions for
Crown Servants (which include anyone on active
military service, the police, &c) in the UK and,
for all I know, for military aircraft in the US.
One that I happen to know about is the issue of
firearms. Crown Servants may possess and use
firearms in the course of their duties without
the requirement to be licensed, unlike the rest of
us, and to the occasional chagrin of innocent
parties slaughtered in their beds by over-
enthusiastic policemen.

Lest you think I digress, I have lived in various
parts of rural Wales for 10 years and have seen
hundreds of military aircraft on exercise &
training, dozens of them at very close quarters
and dozens at night, these last at various speeds
& altitudes while I was out in the fields helping
to diminish the numbers of Mr Fuchs McNab's many
friends & relations. In the UK military aircraft
whizz by at low altitude at night showing only two
lights -- both red, set fore & aft along/below the
fuselage. Depending on the angle (and for all I
know different aircraft have different settings
too) these appear to flash, or not -- depending,
I imagine, on the viewpoint you have of what are
probably revolving lights. The nearest I've been
to one of these was a C-130 flying *below* my
vantage point about 800ft ASL and about 3-400ft
distant. Being quite familiar with Alberts at
close & other ranges, and with the terrain where
this occurred, I'm reasonably sure of the distance.
It carried two flashing (revolving) red beacons
& nothing else. At slightly higher altitudes I've
seen various fast movers similarly lit -- Harriers,
F-15Es, Tornados, Hawks, & Jaguars. All these can
be ID'd with a good night rifle scope. But none
was carrying (or at least had lit) standard nav.
red, green or white lights. (In daylight, for what
it's worth, most fast movers fly with their
landing lights on; the regular Tuesday 7:00pm
3-plane ?SAS? Albert flight over the Preselis in
daylight didn't, but did display std nav lights.)
Much higher, but still not in commercial airspace,
I've also spotted the occasional exec. jet at
night showinging the two red beacons *and* std nav
lights; some general on his way to Belfast, or
wherever, one assumes. Navy Buccaneers also fly
high, for some reason, & I've seen them only in
dalylight, so can't report on their lighting
configuration.

The last time I asked roomful of knowledgeable
Americans, they confirmed that US mil. aircraft
also show two red lights fore & aft at night.
What *else* they may show I didn't ask -- it
wasn't to the purpose at the time.

Whether or not these planes *in the UK* are not
conforming to Federal aviation law, or are observing
an esoteric tradition that ignores any other law
of the air, is neither here nor there. The fact
is, that is how they fly, in my experience, which
may well be more extensive than the average townie's
who has neither sheep nor fowl to protect, and in
addition doesn't normally go to bed at 4:00am, no
matter how many law books he may have to read. So
there is at least the possibility that that is what
Chris Gibson saw. What slightly surprises me is
that Chris was, I understand, once a member of the
ROC, and might be expected to consider military
aricraft lights as a possible solution to his
problem. Is there a reason for that we haven't
heard about?
best wishes
Peter B

At last we're getting somewhere.

I had considered military stuff right from the start, be great if that
explained it, but something doesn't quite gel with that simple explanation.
Most of the military traffic in my area is low / fast / loud. Herks, GR7s
and Tornadoes attacking Bruntingthorpe and they do indeed show the red
lights, but usually a white strobe as well. These were brought in since a
few RAF jets were involved in collisions, same reason the trainers are
painted black. We also get MH-53s, again on the low level. But I think they
are otherwise engaged.

What struck me about these lights was that they didn't look like pinpoints
of light, more like a car tail light or a rounded panel, and of course the
lack of any other lighting. Two single red lights about four finger widths
apart. There was something odd about them that I can't put my finger on.

If it was a single aircraft, why the transverse pair of red lights when you
say that aircraft show a fore and aft pair?

If it was a pair of aircraft would the two lights on each aircraft not be
visible? Especially as they went overhead.

Why would they be flying at what seemed to be medium altitude (ok Larry I
don't know this) in a very busy patch of sky with only these single red
lights.

As I say, military aircraft would be great, but...

Chris

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Fri, 26 Oct 2001 11:05:43 +0200
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Any ideas?

The rules in the UK, set out in the Air Navigation Order and the new JARs,
are the same as those in the US. Indeed, the same rules apply pretty much
the world over, certainly in all ICAO countries.

It may be that military aircraft on exercises may have nav lights turned off
when in designated military training areas. These areas - such as MATZs,
AIAAs, danger, prohibited and restricted areas - are well-defined and shown
on aviation charts, and operations are also often notified by NOTAM, so it
should be easy to check whether this applies. I doubt it in this instance. I
don't have the original message to hand, but if Chris would like to give me
the location again I'd be happy to check it on my half-mil chart.

In any case, you're missing the point. Larry stated that certain aircraft
carry all-red lights as a signal to other aircraft to give way (which means
they would do so outside military areas). My point is that no such provision
or regulation exists. If other pilots (like me) have never heard of such a
rule, there would be no point in having it!

a+
Steve

At 10:36 +0100 25/10/01, rotsky wrote:

>By the way, Larry, the reason I'm so keen
>to get this issue of nav lights sorted is
>that aircraft play such a large role in
>supposed UFO sightings.

[...]

>So I'm not having a go at you... just want to
>get this clear. For the record, here are the
>Federal Aviation Regulations, FAR 25.1385, FAR 25.1397
>and FAR 25.1401, that stipulate lights to be
>carried and their colour:

Hear hear to the first paragraph, but as for the
second... useful, but perhaps not in this case,
which occurred in Leicestershire, England.

No matter what the law may say Joe Public must or
must not do, there are significant exeptions for
Crown Servants (which include anyone on active
military service, the police, &c) in the UK and,
for all I know, for military aircraft in the US.
One that I happen to know about is the issue of
firearms. Crown Servants may possess and use
firearms in the course of their duties without
the requirement to be licensed, unlike the rest of
us, and to the occasional chagrin of innocent
parties slaughtered in their beds by over-
enthusiastic policemen.

Lest you think I digress, I have lived in various
parts of rural Wales for 10 years and have seen
hundreds of military aircraft on exercise &
training, dozens of them at very close quarters
and dozens at night, these last at various speeds
& altitudes while I was out in the fields helping
to diminish the numbers of Mr Fuchs McNab's many
friends & relations. In the UK military aircraft
whizz by at low altitude at night showing only two
lights -- both red, set fore & aft along/below the
fuselage. Depending on the angle (and for all I
know different aircraft have different settings
too) these appear to flash, or not -- depending,
I imagine, on the viewpoint you have of what are
probably revolving lights. The nearest I've been
to one of these was a C-130 flying *below* my
vantage point about 800ft ASL and about 3-400ft
distant. Being quite familiar with Alberts at
close & other ranges, and with the terrain where
this occurred, I'm reasonably sure of the distance.
It carried two flashing (revolving) red beacons
& nothing else. At slightly higher altitudes I've
seen various fast movers similarly lit -- Harriers,
F-15Es, Tornados, Hawks, & Jaguars. All these can
be ID'd with a good night rifle scope. But none
was carrying (or at least had lit) standard nav.
red, green or white lights. (In daylight, for what
it's worth, most fast movers fly with their
landing lights on; the regular Tuesday 7:00pm
3-plane ?SAS? Albert flight over the Preselis in
daylight didn't, but did display std nav lights.)
Much higher, but still not in commercial airspace,
I've also spotted the occasional exec. jet at
night showinging the two red beacons *and* std nav
lights; some general on his way to Belfast, or
wherever, one assumes. Navy Buccaneers also fly
high, for some reason, & I've seen them only in
dalylight, so can't report on their lighting
configuration.

The last time I asked roomful of knowledgeable
Americans, they confirmed that US mil. aircraft
also show two red lights fore & aft at night.
What *else* they may show I didn't ask -- it
wasn't to the purpose at the time.

Whether or not these planes *in the UK* are not
conforming to Federal aviation law, or are observing
an esoteric tradition that ignores any other law
of the air, is neither here nor there. The fact
is, that is how they fly, in my experience, which
may well be more extensive than the average townie's
who has neither sheep nor fowl to protect, and in
addition doesn't normally go to bed at 4:00am, no
matter how many law books he may have to read. So
there is at least the possibility that that is what
Chris Gibson saw. What slightly surprises me is
that Chris was, I understand, once a member of the
ROC, and might be expected to consider military
aricraft lights as a possible solution to his
problem. Is there a reason for that we haven't
heard about?

best wishes
Peter B

From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
Date: Fri, 26 Oct 2001 10:51:21 -0500
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Any ideas?

I'm not saying that it WAS fire balloons, but that you can't yet rule
them out.

All you have is an angular size and an angular velocity. Let's look at
that:

- The reported angular size is much too large to be a single plane,
unless it was flying very low and close. It covers at least 5 full moons.

- The real size, distance, speed, and altitude are all proportional to
each other, with the one restriction being that the distance must be at
least 30 feet. Without other visual aids, there is no way to narrow down
these values.

- There could have been two aircraft. Or the flashing mechanism of the
anticollision lights of one close aircraft may have failed.

- The size and speed if the object had been a mile away is 176 times
the size and speed if it had been 30 feet away.

From: cgibson@skomer.u-net.com
Date: Fri, 26 Oct 2001 20:47:55 GMT
Subject: [UFORL] Re: Any ideas?


Larry, Larry,

I seem to recall my first post on this subject was a question "Any idea
what this is?" You and Jenny (unlike other list members) kindly posted
answers. Even if I disagree (most strongly) with your candelabra
explanation, you did suggest something. As this is a UFO list I would have
thought such "lights in the sky" cases would be commonplace, but apparently
not.

Jenny's theory is plausible, but I suspect that practice has been stamped
out, especially in busy airspace. Pete's military aircraft theory is
probably correct, but I have not seen such lights on the military aircraft
in this area before, but I don't live in a designated low flying area, so
the anti-collision beacons may be required around Leics.

As an aside, lighting patterns, like sound and contrails are not considered
 valid recognition features for aircraft. Therefore any aircraft whose
lights were seen would only be reported or logged as "lights". Aircraft
sound, would be "heard, not seen". Consequently I wouldn't even attempt to
identify an aircraft from its lights, unless it was by having a good view
of the "Logo" lights.

Same goes for contrails. The old joke is: On asked to identify the source
of some contrails, the chap replied "It is either a B-52, two Nimrods, four
Phantoms or four Lightnings flying on their sides."

So to conclude: If a pair of red lights are military aircraft, it would
appear that the triangular patterns of red lights seen in the past are also
military aircraft flying in formation. Have we nailed the big Triangles?

Again.

Chris

Chris,

I haven't had time to comment on this before now - there are a
number of possibly comparative reports, including at least one
from the UK!

An online search for 'ufo' and 'two red lights' brings up several
cases. The UK one I noticed was:

Red Lights Off Coast Leave Mystery

Coastguards have been puzzled by a series of red flare-like
lights spotted in the Bristol Channel off the coast of Somerset,
England, on the night of December 14.

The Portishead lifeboat was launched following dozens of 999
callers reported two red lights off the coast at Clevedon.

But no sign of any persons or vessel in distress had been found
after three hours of searching.
[END]


Also from:

http://www.msatech.com/nuforc/webreports/S17280.html

8 April, 2001

Two fast moving red lights observed from the ground manuevering
in formation near aircraft in Northeastern Florida.

Looking at a relatively clear Northwest evening sky (some
scattered light haze) I observed what I surmised to be a slow
moving aircraft turn on it's very bright white landing lights on
an apparent approach to Daytona Airport which was a few miles to
the South of my location near the intersection of Florida SR 40
and SR A1A in Ormond Beach. After observing the aircraft for
about 15 seconds I saw two small round dull red lights, many
hundreds of yards apart, appeared over the airplane at 45 degrees
above the horizon. The two red lights moved perfectly in unison,
first moving away from each other, then almost converging and
finally travelling at their original spacing before disappearing
near tree top level to the West. The two red lights had a unique
deep dull red hue which did not change in color or intensity. The
lights movements through the sky approximated the shape of an
hour glass. No noise was heard from the lights. The two red
lights were visible for 10 seconds. After the red lights
disappeared the landing lights from the plane (helicopter?)
switched off and the aircraft disappeared into the evening sky.
[END]

There are many other 'UFO' cases where 'two red lights' feature.

Just over a year later the dark triangle returned. October 1992,

...Shortly after, near Trollhattan, Jeanette looked up towards

Chris,

I haven't had time to comment on this before now - there are a
number of possibly comparative reports, including at least one
from the UK!

An online search for 'ufo' and 'two red lights' brings up several
cases. The UK one I noticed was:

Red Lights Off Coast Leave Mystery

Coastguards have been puzzled by a series of red flare-like
lights spotted in the Bristol Channel off the coast of Somerset,
England, on the night of December 14.

The Portishead lifeboat was launched following dozens of 999
callers reported two red lights off the coast at Clevedon.

But no sign of any persons or vessel in distress had been found
after three hours of searching.
[END]


Also from:

http://www.msatech.com/nuforc/webreports/S17280.html

8 April, 2001

Two fast moving red lights observed from the ground manuevering
in formation near aircraft in Northeastern Florida.

Looking at a relatively clear Northwest evening sky (some
scattered light haze) I observed what I surmised to be a slow
moving aircraft turn on it's very bright white landing lights on
an apparent approach to Daytona Airport which was a few miles to
the South of my location near the intersection of Florida SR 40
and SR A1A in Ormond Beach. After observing the aircraft for
about 15 seconds I saw two small round dull red lights, many
hundreds of yards apart, appeared over the airplane at 45 degrees
above the horizon. The two red lights moved perfectly in unison,
first moving away from each other, then almost converging and
finally travelling at their original spacing before disappearing
near tree top level to the West. The two red lights had a unique
deep dull red hue which did not change in color or intensity. The
lights movements through the sky approximated the shape of an
hour glass. No noise was heard from the lights. The two red
lights were visible for 10 seconds. After the red lights
disappeared the landing lights from the plane (helicopter?)
switched off and the aircraft disappeared into the evening sky.
[END]

There are many other 'UFO' cases where 'two red lights' feature.


>So to conclude: If a pair of red lights are military aircraft,
>it would appear that the triangular patterns of red lights seen
>in the past are also military aircraft flying in formation. Have
>we nailed the big Triangles?

Just over a year later the dark triangle returned. October 1992,
and Mr Marcel Westerlund and his partner Jeanette Norell and
their kids, Kristoffer and Sebastian, were driving down to
Stenungsund [Sweden] on the west coast.

...Shortly after, near Trollhattan, Jeanette looked up towards

our car!" Marcel pulled over and looked up. He said: "I felt like
that guy in the movie "Close Encounters of the Third Kind", when
I saw two large red lights at the centre of the bottom of a huge,
flying triangle".

Completely silent, the triangle passed over their car...

It crossed the road, flew towards the edge of the woods and stood
hovering just above the tree tops.

...After a while, the family got tired and drove off into the
night.
[END]
Do you think... Nah...couldn't have been.

From: "rotsky" <rotsky@wanadoo.fr>
Date: Tue, 30 Oct 2001 15:22:19 +0100
Subject: RE: [UFORL] Re: Any ideas?

Just a couple of observations on Chris' sighting, for what they're worth.
Just trying to add some data.

The position of 52 29N and 001 09W puts the location at just under 1 statute
mile WSW of Bruntingthorpe aerodrome, 2-ish miles North of Lutterworth (I
assume there's some margin of error in this).

Six miles to the SE is Husbands Bosworth, which is marked as an area of
intense gliding activity.

There is no MATZ, AIAA, danger, prohibited or restricted zone in the
immediate vicinity. Class A controlled airspace above starts at FL55
(5500ft - the Daventry CTA) or FL75 depending on the exact location.
Otherwise, it's in the open FIR (uncontrolled airspace). Cottesmore and
Wittering air bases are to the NE, and Wittering's extended centreline runs
right through the location.

Like I say, for what it's worth...

a+
Steve

If I recall correctly, Arnold's first sketch was made on the back
of an envelope, almost directly after his sighting. This was
shown to his fellow pilots at Yakima, where Arnold stopped on the
way to Pendleton.

unsourced item is the drawing shown on that aforementioned UFO
video, when the Arnold case is featured.

suggest any other explanation and it does resemble his earlier
depiction of a 'crescent-shape' - as he originally described the
objects.

some writing which is partly illegible. Beneath the objects he's
written 'Black' and then something I can't decipher.

Arnold might be emphasising that the objects had a darker front
'wing-tip' - he places a separate line at the edge of each
individual drawing.

If anyone can make sense of what Arnold has written here, please
let us know.

From: KRandle993@aol.com
Date: Thu, 8 Nov 2001 08:35:10 EST
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Discovery Channel (UK)

Good Morning -

>The "black sergeant" common in some of the Roswell tales is
>unlikely in 1947, since the USAF did not integrate their units.

Actually, President Truman ordered the integration of the units in
September, 1947, which is, of course, a couple of months too late.
However, there were all black units, commanded by white officers,
very much in evidence in July, 1947. At Roswell, for example,
Squadron S was made up of black soldiers, commanded by white
officers.

Black units in the American military have a long and proud history,
starting with the 54th Massachusetts during the Civil War, which was
involved in the attack on Fort Wagner, the 9th and 10th US Cavalry
which fought with distinction in the old west, and the fighter squadrons
trained during the Second World War.

What this means is that there could easily have been a white, red-haired
captain working with a black sergeant in July, 1947. Although it is
unlikely, it is certainly within the realm of possibility.

>It would also seem unlikely, that at the time of the incident, a
>black man would talk to white person in this manner.
>[END]

Given the time, 1947, this is a much more likely reason to doubt
Dennis' story. I found it difficult to believe that a white officer would
stand by as a black sergeant threatened a white civilian. This smacks
of a tale invented in the late 1980s rather than a memory from the
1940s.


[snip]

>Do you conclude that not one of Glenn's related claims is true,
>i.e., that he never witnessed 'Roswell' debris on base, or was
>threatened, escorted off base, or that the 'red haired Captain'
>and 'black Sergeant' existed?

My opinion, based on the research I have conducted, in many interviews
with Glenn Dennis, the search for the nurse that I, and many others such
as Vic Golubic and Ted Oliphant, have conducted, the lack of corroborative
detail, and the shifting nature of the story, is that Glenn Dennis is an
opportunist who was not directly involved, had no nurse friend, saw no
alien debris, and created his tale out of thin air (or heard other stories and
interjected himself into them). I don't believe he was threatened by a red-
haired captain or black NCO. I believe he is just another wannabe who dots
the historical landscape like Gerald Anderson and Brushy Bill Roberts (he's
the guy who, in 1950, claimed that he was the real Billy the Kid).

KRandle

<p class=MsoNormal align=center style='text-align:center'><span lang=EN-US

<p class=MsoNormal align=center style='text-align:center'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-family:Arial;mso-bidi-font-family:"Times New Roman";mso-ansi-

<h1><span lang=EN-US style='mso-ansi-language:EN-US'>ICEFALLS
INVESTIGATED BY
THE ANOMALY FOUNDATION<o:p></o:p></span></h1>

<p class=MsoNormal align=center style='text-align:center'><b style='mso-bidi-font-
weight:
normal'><span lang=EN-US style='font-size:14.0pt;mso-bidi-font-size:12.0pt;
font-family:Arial;mso-bidi-font-family:"Times New Roman";mso-ansi-language:
EN-US'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></b></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText><span lang=EN-US>The “Anomaly Foundation” pushes
research
on the falls of iceblocks reported in Spain</span></p>
<p class=MsoBodyText><span lang=EN-
US><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>In the threshold of the second anniversary of the
strange ice rock shower phenomenon which took place in numerous Spanish<span
style='color:green'> </span>locations in January 2000, the not-for-profit
organization Anomaly Foundation (Apartado 5041, 39080 Santander, Spain) will
finance a documentary compilation on this subject. “Hydroaerolites: the enigma
which fell out of the blue” will be the title of a report which is being
prepared under the editorship of telecommunications engineer Manuel Borraz. It
received the 2001 “Universitas” scholarship, sponsored by the Foundation with
the participation of the Washington-based Fund for UFO Research. It is trusted
that the mystery which impacted many Spaniards and world-wide media, becoming
the<span style='color:green'> </span>target for hoaxes and speculations as well
as for many esoteric explanations, can be finally placed into its real
historical context and proper perspective with this new
publication.<o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>This set of controversial episodes, which were
followed by cloned events in Italy and Holland, had at the start the simple
journalist name of iceblocks, but the Foundation provided the more scientific
denomination of hydroaerolites, meaning rocks made of water which fall from the
sky.<o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>Manuel Borraz, the leader of the project, declared
that “one of the objectives of this collective monograph will be to reflect the
present status of the question about the origin of these masses of ice which
allegedly<span style='color:green'> </span>fell in many scattered villages”. As
it is well-known, many of these occurrences proved to be frauds. Although there
were some<span style='color:green'> </span>experts who pointed to ordinary
meteorological origins such as hail or the natural production of ice on aircraft,
this phenomenon arose considerable interest among the mainstream Spanish
scientific community with an intense debate, still unresolved, which resulted
in the creation of a research committee by the Consejo Superior de
Investigaciones Cientificas (CSIC), the upper scientific research council of
the Spanish academia.<o:p></o:p></span></p>
<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>The Anomaly Foundation was founded 1997 with the aim
to fund the<span style='color:green'> </span>scientific-oriented investigation
of unusual aerial phenomena, commonly called UFOs, to preserve the related
documentation gathered in Spain in the last 50 years, to provide scholarships,
grants and prizes, and to publish specialized journals and
books.<o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText><span lang=EN-US style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>On the weekend of November 2 to 4, the Foundation
Board and collaborators met in Valencia. Four field work funds were granted to
Spanish researchers who during this year accomplished good case investigations
of UFO experiences: Marcos Benítez Campillo (Proyecto CREBE, Cádiz), Antonio
Salinas (SIB, Granada), Juan Carlos Victorio (Guipúzcoa) and Carlos León
(Asturias).<o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>In the last years, the Anomaly Foundation, whose web
site <a href="http://www.anomalia.org/"><b>www.anomalia.org</b></a> has
already<span
style='color:green'> </span>received more than 100,000 visits, has become a
routine reference on this subject-matter, specially for the university
environment, because of its development of data bases on UFO report data,
scientific references bibliographies, etc.<o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-weight:normal'>November 2001<o:p></o:p></span></p>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p
>

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
style='font-
weight:normal'><![if !supportEmptyParas]>&nbsp;<![endif]><o:p></o:p></span></p

<p class=MsoBodyText style='text-align:justify'><span lang=EN-US
