I would still suspect this feature in the footage had its origins
within Glenn Dennis' 'severed hand' story, which presumably did
pre-date the film's [5 May, 1995] appearance. Curiously, there's
an interview with Glenn Dennis in which he doesn't mention the
'severed hand' in his descriptions, however, what he does reveal
is a specific detail about the alleged nurse, claiming she was a
2nd Lt.

That interview is contained within a video, 'UFO Secret, The
Roswell Crash' [and possibly elsewhere]. I had transcribed this a
few years ago and, for the record, Dennis states:

"...and this was a young 2nd Lieutenant, had only been in the
service less than three months and commissioned less than three
months. A very deeply religious lady, she was born and raised in
a very strict catholic family, attended all the private catholic
schools, pre-school and high schools and her folks wanted her to
become a nun.

...and she says 'I can't believe what I've just seen'. She said
'this was the most horrible thing I've ever seen in my life'. She
was going into this examination room that was across the hall,
she was going in to get some supplies and when she walked in the
door there was 2 doctors there and she noticed a horrible smell
immediately, but she saw these 2 doctors and they said 'we need
you'. She started out the door and they said 'you stay here,
we've got to have you' and what it was, they were examining, she
told me 3 bodies, foreign bodies, and she said 2 of them were
very mutilated."

[NARRATIVE] ACCORDING TO MR DENNIS, JUDY AND BOTH DOCTORS
BECAME
ILL FROM THE STENCH OF THE BODIES AS THEY CONTINUED TO
EXAMINE
THEM. JUDY WAS STILL NOT WELL THE FOLLOWING DAY WHEN GLEN
MET HER
FOR LUNCH AT THE OFFICERS CLUB. BUT HE WAS MORE DISTURBED BY
HER
EMOTIONAL STATE.

" ...she was almost in a state of shock because she said it was
so gruesome, so horrible and she would almost grab her head (in
despair). It looked like she was just going into total shock".

"She had drawn me just a little the night before, she had a
description of an arm that she had drawn and the anatomy of the
arm, which was different from ours, there was only 4 fingers on
the hand, didn't have a thumb to it, only 4 very slim fragile
little fingers, that when they turned one of the hands over they
noticed at the end of the fingers there was like little pads on
each one of the 4 fingers there and it looked to them like they
were like little suction cups, they were little hollowed out
areas that looked kinda like a suction cup.

The heads on these individuals were much larger, somewhat larger
than a human head would be, the eyes were very sunken, there
wasn't a convex nose or anything, the nose was very concave with
only 2 little orifices, the ears..there was no ear, there only
might be 2 little orifices on the side but very small little
lobes, it looked like they might function or might close maybe,
or whatever, but they was very small, nothing resembling the ear
on a human anatomy at all.

She never touched her food at all, I think I drank my coke but I
was so..I thought 'my God, this was something else'. Then she
said 'I've got to go back to the barracks', she said 'I am
deathly ill and I've got to go back to the barracks' and
then..that was the last time I ever saw her.

The next day I called...I was really concerned on what was
happening to her and they told me that she wasn't working, that
she was unavailable that day. And so, the next day I made the
call again, I made 2 or 3 calls the next day and it was also she
was still unavailable. Then the third day, I called and they said
that she'd been transferred out and they didn't know where, but
she was no longer there at the air base.

...FOR DAYS GLEN KEPT ASKING QUESTIONS, BUT GOT NO ANSWERS.

"Well then, maybe about ten days to 2 weeks or so later I get a
letter from her in the mail, addressed to the funeral home and
all it was, it was just a note, said 'I can't write, I don't have
time to write now, but here's an APO number you can send me the
mail to'. She also told me 'I am in London'.

..it was at least 2 weeks, maybe 3 weeks later, the letter that I
had sent to her with the APO number was returned to me and on the
envelope it said 'Return to Sender' and it had a big red print,
it said 'Deceased'."
[END OF EXTRACT]


It's some story if there's zero factual basis.

By any default, I would have to go along with Tim Printy's
conclusion [http://members.aol.com/TPrinty/Dennis.html] - that
Dennis was calling upon memories from a number of later events.

However, as Dennis places the entire narrative within a short,
consecutive timeframe - indeed more so, as in various interviews
he provides an intricate, overall account - it's alternatively
disturbing to rationalise that he deliberately made this entire,
convoluted story up.

A couple of points which could be cited in his defence:

1. Although there wasn't a rank of 'Airman' at that time, I
wouldn't be concerned to hear Dennis retrospectively describe the
injured serviceman he took to base as an 'airman'.

2. Threats from a 'black Sergeant' - has that possibly been
misconstrued? There's an informative interview with Karl Pflock,
on behalf of OMNI, which is online at:

http://www.omnimag.com/archives/open_book/roswell/star.html

An extract:

OMNI: Did they physically manhandle you as has been reported?

DENNIS: Oh, no. They weren't roughing me up or anything. They
were real nice. But then we'd only gone a few feet when a voice
said, "Bring that SOB back here." We turned around and there was
this big, redheaded captain, about six three or four, with a real
short crew cut and the meanest eyes I'd ever seen, like the devil
himself looking at me. He had with him a black sergeant who was
holding a clipboard.

OMNI: Where did they come from?

DENNIS: Somebody went and got them, I guess. Anyway, the captain
came up to me and poked a finger in my chest and said, "Look,
mister, you don't go into Roswell and start a bunch of rumors
that there's been a crash. Nothing has happened here, you
understand?" And he kept poking me. Of course, I was getting a
little upset. I said, "I'm a civilian and you can't do anything
to me. You can go to hell!" That's when he jabbed me again and
said, "Somebody will be picking your bones out of the sand." Then
the sergeant said, "Sir, he would make better dog food." So I
popped off at him, too. Then the captain said, "Get the son of a
bitch out of here," and the MPs started taking me back down the
hall again.
[END]

A significantly different scenario; the Sergeant doesn't verbally
abuse Dennis, instead, he directs his 'supportive' comments to
the Captain.

That might have being permissible.


For what it's worth, an observation relating to Glenn Dennis'
interview with Karl.

Dennis states: "I received a phone call from the Roswell Army Air
Field mortuary officer on July 7 sometime after lunch, around
one-thirty. I have no idea who it was, but he asked if we had any
baby caskets, three foot six or four foot, hermetically sealed".

This implies the 'bodies' had been discovered by that time.

Dennis apparently confirms the timeline when Karl asks:
"Returning to 1947, after meeting with the nurse [the following
day - James], you had no doubt there was something very much out
of line going on. When did you see the newspaper with the
captured saucer story?".

The 'captured saucer' headline first appeared on 8 July and
Dennis replies: "About six or seven that night I went in to write
an obituary, and the paper was lying on the desk at Ballard's. I
picked it up, saw the headline, and thought, 'Maybe that's what
she's gotten into!'".

As Marcel and Cavitt didn't return with debris from the Foster
ranch until late on the evening of 7 July, where, when and how
were those 'Glenn Dennis autopsy' bodies discovered earlier that
morning, or in previous days?

"According to the US Air Force, there were only five nurses at

there. According to Dennis, she was, 'real cute, like a small

The AF report states that in 1947, Eileen Fanton was single,
5'1", and weighed 100 pounds, had black hair, dark eyes, and was
of Italian descent. Dennis had made remarks that she was
catholic. Her records revealed this as well. The AF investigation
also revealed that she served in London, England from 1952 to
1955. Even more amazing is that she left Roswell on September 4,

nurse but there appears to be nothing mysterious about the events
in her career".

In his interview with Karl Pflock, Dennis confirms she was,
"about 23 and real cute -- like a small Audrey Hepburn, with
short black hair, dark eyes, and olive skin...".

Specifically, Dennis further highlights the nurse to be, "A very
deeply religious lady, she was born and raised in a very strict
catholic family, attended all the private catholic schools, pre-
school and high schools and her folks wanted her to become a
nun".

If Eileen Fanton was of Italian descent, that could concur with
an 'olive skin' and someone who had conceivably been brought up
in the "strict" catholic tradition.

Again... there were statedly only five nurses on base at this
time and keeping in mind the anomalies with Glenn Dennis being
able to identify his nurse... It has to be, at least, a
remarkable coincidence and, definitely, Eileen Fanton must be a
'best bet'.


Whilst one, profoundly, hesitates to remark on the evidence for
remnants of an underlying... how can we best put it...
'unfulfilled relationship' involved here, clearly, Glenn enjoyed
the regular company of this nurse - "about 23 and real cute --
like a small Audrey Hepburn, with short black hair, dark eyes,
and olive skin...".

However, we must, absolutely, appreciate he clarified to Karl:

OMNI: Many questions have been raised about your relationship
with the nurse, even that you and she considered marriage.

DENNIS: That's bull! I was married, and she and I were just
friendly acquaintances, nothing else. I wasn't after her or
anything. When all this happened, she'd been at the base only
about three months, in the service about seven. She was about 23
and real cute -- like a small Audrey Hepburn, with short black
hair, dark eyes, and olive skin -- but kind of a loner, shy,
didn't fit in. But I talked with her whenever I saw her at the
infirmary, so I got to know a little about her.
[END]

I hope that sets Glenn's perspective in context. Karl merely
asked the obvious question...

to reveal what she had told him.

A year or two later Dennis asked me why we hadn't found his nurse. He had
given us her name. Later still he told Karl Pflock that her name was Naomi
Maria Selff, which isn't that different, and Pflock couldn't find her.

I might mention here that in the search I conducted included reveiwing the
New York Times index for the aircraft accident that Dennis said killed her, a
reveiw of various financial records, state archives and with the help of a
police
officer, a full credit check for her. We failed to find a trace. I tried to
get the Army
to turn loose the morning reports for the medical staff at Roswell but failed.
Vic Golubic, after months, finally did succeed, and they revealed nothing of a
nurse named Self. When finally confronted with this negative information,
back in 1997, Dennis said that he had never given anyone the correct name.

At that point, I decided that the Glenn Dennis tale was not grounded in
reality
and that his nurse did not exist. He compells us, for years, to look for her
under
one name and when we tell him that no one served as an Army nurse under that
name, he claimed that he hadn't given us the real name and refuses to help
with
the search from that point.

So, the Air Force believes that his nurse was Eileen Fanton. I believe there
was
no nurse, so the search beyond that is of no value and Air Force speculations,
which, I believe have some support inside the UFO community are without
foundation. Fanton is not Dennis' nurse because she didn't exist.
This, I believe answers the question.

Good Evening -

 >You missed my point. With so many similarities between Fanton and Nurse

But you see, we had the name. Dennis insisted for years that it was
Naomi Self or Naomi Selff. Within hours of telling me the story of his
involvement, he had given me the name. He reinforced it repeatedly, saying
that her name was Self, that she was from Minnesota, that she was a
young nurse and that she was killed in a plane crash just months after
the 1947 UFO crash. And, he told everyone else that her name was Self.

Second, the fact that she did not appear in the Yearbook was never an
important consideration. Walter Haut told me that 10 to 20 percent of the
people assigned to the base in July 1947 didn't appear in the Yearbook.
The practical demonstration of this was when Bill Moore rejected the
testimony of Pappy Henderson because he didn't find Henderson's name
in the Yearbook... turns out that Henderson is in there, as a member of a
flight crew, but not in the individual section.

We, and by this I include Vic Golubic, learned that there were about 20
women who could be considered nurses at Roswell in 1947, but only 5
were listed in the Yearbook.

So, we had the name, a name that Dennis insisted was the right one, and
we had no reason to apply the description he gave to any of the nurses
pictured because none of them had the right name, or one that was even
close... Not to mention the fact, we had shown him the Yearbook
and he said that she wasn't there, so Fanton was eliminated at this point.

So, there was no point in looking at the nurses who were pictured in the
Yearbook... none were the right ones and none had the right name. We took
the investigation in a different direction, searching for any corroboration
that
there had ever been an Army nurse named Naomi Self, all the while, Dennis
was telling us that was her name. Just why would we have looked anywhere
else? And, when we proved the negative, when we could say with confidence
that there had never been an Army nurse named Naomi Self (except perhaps
during the Civil War which would have made her waaaay too old), we told
this to Dennis. At that point he changed the story and changed the name of
the nurse and at that point I realized that nothing he said about this could
be trusted.

So, Fanton matched his description, to a limited degree but of course,
Fanton was a First Lieutenant, not a Second Lieutenant, Fanton had been in
the Army for nearly two years, not three months, she was not fairly new to
Roswell, and because Dennis failed to identify her in the Yearbook, there
was no reason to pursue this line of investigation. That others seem to
believe
there were similarities is irrelevant and the Air Force opinion that Fanton
might be Dennis' nurse is irrelevant because she was not his nurse and the
tale being told was not based in reality.

See, we really did look at this closely.

KRandle

nurse, and although she bore a passing resemblance to Dennis' description, so
did Natalie Wood... and I would much rather have chased her than Fanton, but
she wasn't Dennis' nurse either"

And if Dennis was lying about the original name why do you think he would say
that Fanton was his nurse, when you could actually check up on her story and
found it that he was lying. If Dennis was using Fanton as a model for his
tall tale, then he certainly would not tell you when you presented her
picture to him. You would then have discovered that his tale was false.
Instead he strung you guys along for some time before it became obvious that
he was lying.

"And since this is becoming redundant, I now quietly bow out..."

Understood and agreed.

Tim

<BR><A
HREF="http://hometown.aol.com.au/GlenUNSW/mtDNA/RootShaft.jpg">http://ww
w4.tpgi.com.au/ufoesa/dna_root&amp;shaft.JPG</A>
<BR>
<BR></FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">a). Root sample mtDNA differences.</FONT><FONT
COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">
<BR> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;4 Bases = bp 16223, 16255, 16278 &amp; 16254
<BR> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(<I>Basque Gaelic</I>).
<BR>
<BR></FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">b). Shaft sample mtDNA differences.</FONT><FONT
COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">
<BR> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;5 Bases = bp 16108, 16129, 16162, 16172 &amp; 16304
<BR> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(<I>Chinese Mongoloid</I>).
<BR>
<BR>Only one type of mtDNA sequence should be observed per
<BR>individual. However, a condition, known as
<BR></FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0"><B>"Heteroplasmy"</FONT><FONT
COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial"
LANG="0"></B> can occur and is defined as more than
<BR>one mtDNA type being carried by an individual.
<BR>
<BR></FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">(See Ref below R4 - R10).</FONT><FONT
COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">
<BR>
<BR>An individual is </FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2
FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial"
LANG="0"><B>"Heteroplasmic"</FONT><FONT COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2
FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0"></B> if his mtDNA sequence
<BR>differs slightly (usually at just one base position)
<BR>from cell to cell in his body.
<BR>
<BR>It can theoretically occur anywhere in the mtDNA
<BR>genome, although hotspot positions have been observed.
<BR>
<BR>If two samples demonstrate sequence concordance, or a
<BR>common base at every position, they cannot be excluded
<BR>as coming from the same source (no error).
<BR>
<BR></FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">OR:</FONT><FONT COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2
FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">
<BR>
<BR>Because of heteroplasmy, a difference between the known
<BR>and questioned samples of a single (1) base pair (bp)
<BR>is not sufficient to result in an </FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2
FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">"Exclusion"</FONT><FONT
COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">.
<BR>
<BR>The FBI deems such results </FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2
FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial"
LANG="0">"Inconclusive"</FONT><FONT COLOR="#000000" SIZE=2
FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">.
<BR>
<BR></FONT><FONT COLOR="#ff0000" SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF"
FACE="Arial" LANG="0">HOWEVER:</FONT><FONT COLOR="#000000"
SIZE=2 FAMILY="SANSSERIF" FACE="Arial" LANG="0">
<BR>
<BR>A difference of 2 base pairs (bp) or more is required

From: KRandle993@aol.com
Date: Thu, 15 Nov 2001 16:56:44 EST
Subject: Re: [UFORL] Discovery Channel (UK)

Good Afternoon -

The whole Ragsdale story was told in THE ROSWELL ENCYCLOPEDIA. I have
taken that entry and condensed it to answer the questions. This might be a
little disjointed as I deleted some long sections that don't really identify
the
discrepancies.

KRandle

On January 26, 1993, Jim Ragsdale told UFO researchers, for the first time,
in some detail, how he had witnessed the crash of an alien spacecraft in July
1947, how he had watched the military begin the recovery operation, and how
he, with a female companion, originally identified as Trudy Truelove, had
picked up pieces of the strange metallic debris.

Don Schmitt had arranged to meet with Ragsdale and his wife at their home to
discuss the story and he recorded the interview on audio tape.

Schmitt had been to the impact site north of town during the trip so he had
photographs of it. Trying to make sure that Ragsdale was describing the same
place, Schmitt showed Ragsdale pictures of the terrain. Looking at the
photographs of the site north of Roswell, Ragsdale said, "That right there
looks like the place right there."

Ragsdale then said, "But what I figure, I figure there's two spaceships and
when one came down they just picked up what they could and just left the rest
of them. But it was either dummies or bodies or something there. They looked
like bodies. They weren't very long... over four or five foot long at most.
We didn't see their faces or nothing like that there, but we had just got to
the site and we heard the Army, the sirens and stuff all coming and we got
into the damn jeep and taking off. We had to hold a fence up and go up under
the damn fence onto another ranch to come out from there."

Schmitt asked, "How far would you say this is from outside of town here?"

Ragsdale replied, "Oh hell, what? Forty miles... It's a good thirty to forty
miles."

And again in July 1993, Schmitt and Randle met with Ragsdale with the hope of
a video taped interview. Ragsdale didn't want to sit down for it, but did
discuss the case again.

In September 1994, the Ragsdale story took a new turn. Max Littell, of the
International UFO Museum and Research Center in Roswell, had been keeping in
close contact with Ragsdale since he was introduced to the Ragsdale family by
Schmitt. Now the tale told by Ragsdale was beginning to shift significantly.

But now it had changed radically. According to it, the object passed through
the trees to impact less than a hundred yards from where his truck had been
parked. Ragsdale and his friend took flashlights and walked over, spending
"considerable time looking around."

Now, rather than seeing bodies or dummies in the distance, Ragsdale was close
enough to touch them. They were dressed in silver uniforms and wore a tight
helmets. Ragsdale now claimed that he tried to remove one of the helmets but
couldn't. The eyes, according to Ragsdale, were large and oval and didn't
resemble anything human. Later still he would suggest that the skin of the
dead alien beings was gray.

In this interview Ragsdale said that it wasn't too long before they heard
what they believed were trucks and heavy equipment coming. "We left and were
not there when whatever it was arrived." This is, of course, in direct
conflict with the detailed descriptions of the convoy offered by Ragsdale in
earlier interviews.

Describing how to find the impact site, Ragsdale now said, "A sign post on
the Pine Lodge Road indicates '53 miles to Roswell.' Near this sign is a road
going south toward Pine Lodge... and the turn off to Arabella leads east and
south. Two or 3 miles down this road towards Arabella is the site of our
pickup that night and nearby is the impact site."

The changes in the tale told by Ragsdale were detailed in The Jim Ragsdale
Story, written by Max Littell.

The statement made on January 27, 1993 said:
On a night during July, 1947, I, James Ragsdale, was in the company of a
woman in an area approximately forty (40) miles northwest of Roswell, New
Mexico during a severe lightning storm. I and my companion observed a bright
flash and what appeared to be a bright light source moving to the southeast.
Later, at sunrise, driving in that direction, I and my companion came upon a
ravine near a bluff that was covered with pieces of unusual wreckage, remains
of a damaged craft and a number of smaller bodied beings outside the craft.
While observing the scene, I and my companion watched as a military convoy
arrived and secured the scene. As a result of the convoy's appearance we
quickly fled the area. I hereby swear the aforementioned account is accurate
and true to the best of my knowledge and recollection.

Ragsdale signed it and Littell notarized it. He sent the original to Randle,
but kept copies in the files of the International UFO Museum. They were in
the process of acquiring files about the Roswell case.

After that Littell began talking with Ragsdale frequently. It was important
that Ragsdale identify the exact location of the crash and Littell said he
would drive him out. In the "Max Littell Meets Jim Ragsdale," chapter of The
Jim Ragsdale Story, he is quoted as saying:
Believing the alleged impact site to be only 30 miles from Roswell, I offered
to take a doctor and nurse, along with oxygen. Since the site was only 30
miles from Roswell, I thought we could be out and back in two hours.
At this point, Ragsdale told me, "It is not 30 miles to the site because it
is 53 mile to the turn-off." I replied, "Fifty-three miles out on Highway 285
to Albuquerque would put you two thirds of the way to Vaughn." Ragsdale
responded, "It's not 285 but Highway 48, Pine Lodge Road."

The question is how did Ragsdale, who had spoken to Randle four times about
the case, and who was recorded by Schmitt, get from a site thirty to forty
miles north of town to one where the turn off is more than fifty? When they
interviewed him, why did he insist the site was much closer to town? And why
did he identify it from photographs which look nothing like the terrain
around Pine Lodge that he was now describing to Littell?

This is a major change in the story. The problem comes back to Ragsdale. Not
only had he identified the site from photographs shown to him by Schmitt, but
he also used a map. In fact, and according to Schmitt, in an attempt to help
locate the site today, he mentioned that it was close to the El Paso Natural
Gas Pipeline which runs north of town today. That is not to suggest that he
was working on that line, or that it existed in 1947.

The problem with Ragsdale's identification of the Pine Lodge site are the
statements made by those who lived in the Pine Lodge area in 1947. Of those
interviewed not a single one talked about this event. In fact, Littell
suggested in June 1996 that a reporter for The Roswell Daily Record should
check to see if anyone out in the Pine Lodge a
rea remembered anything. That research failed to produce any corroboration.
Littell, "Freely acknowledged that Ragsdale Production, Inc. [headed up by
Littell's son-in-law] never tried to find or talk to any of these people
[residents of the Pine Lodge area]. 'As far as we were concerned, this story
of Ragsdale is valid,' said Littell. 'What am I trying to prove he's lying
for? We're not going to do that. You go ahead and prove he's lying. I'm just
telling you what the man said.'"

Littell did secure a second notarized statement for Ragsdale. That would mean
that there were now two sworn statements available that seemed to contradict
one another.

Barrett, in his attempt to be as thorough as possible checked all this out.
He noticed that the longer, second, first-person statement contained a
significant number of different details. Besides changing the site to near
the Pine Lodge, Ragsdale was talking of a nocturnal visit to the crashed
craft where he even tried to pull a helmet off one of the bodies.

But the important point, according to Barrett, was "In addition to the
varying detail, Ragsdale's second statement had another problem. The document
carried the seal of notary Kathy Weaver of Logan County, Oklahoma - home of
Ragsdale's daughter, Judy Lott - along with Weaver's written declaration that
the two-page document was 'subscribed and sworn to before me this 15th day of
April, 1995.' Weaver admitted that Ragsdale didn't actually sign the
statement in her presence. 'I swear to God he did not,' she said."

Apparently what happened, according to Barrett's story is that Weaver added
her signature and embossed notarial seal after Judy Lott, a co-employee of
the same firm where Weaver worked, brought the document, already signed to
Weaver's office. Because she knew Lott, she notarized the statement. Weaver
agreed, again according to Barrett's story, that it's "bad practice for
notaries to attest to a signature not written while they're watching but that
'we do it all the time.'"

This procedure, under legal precedent, invalidates the force of the
notarization. According to Barrett, "All that remains is an unsworn statement
- a mere piece of paper, really - without the added credibility that it has
been rendered in the presence of Almighty God subject to the laws of false
swearing and even perjury."

Judy Lott denied that Ragsdale had signed the statement without a notary
present. In fact, she told Barrett, "We had the notary come to our home
because Dad was too ill and couldn't leave the house." But then, confronted
with the information that the notary had denied ever meeting her father and
hadn't witnessed the signature, Lott acknowledged that her father had not
signed it in front of the notary. In fact, according to other information,
Ragsdale might not have even been in Oklahoma when the affidavit was signed.

With the second statement invalidated, it meant that the only affidavit left
was the one that was based on Schmitt's tape recorded interview in early
1994. In an ironic twist it was Max Littell who was the notary on the first
statement. It meant that he was the witness to the Ragsdale signature on the
only valid affidavit.

In 1998, Jim Houran and Stephen Porter reviewed the Ragsdale story using a
technique they labeled Statement Validity Analysis (SVA). Using the
statements made be Ragsdale, specifically, those made in the second affidavit
and in the text of The Jim Ragsdale Story, they analyzed the information
using both SVA and Fact Pattern Analysis.

Under the criterion for the SVA it was concluded, "The results of this
statement analysis indicate that the Ragsdales accounts were not credible
according to know features of memories for true events."

The same conclusion was reached when the fact pattern analysis was applied to
the Ragsdale tale. It was noted, "The results of this fact pattern analysis
indicate that the Ragsdale accounts are not credible [emphasis in original]
in that they exhibit major factual inconsistencies and, independent of the
nature of the event itself, include potential implausible information."

In the final conclusions, Houran and Porter wrote, "SAV and fact pattern
analysis by the second author [Porter] suggested that "The Jim Ragsdale
Story" is not credible. We argue, therefore, that the story represents either
a deliberate fabrication or false memories of imagined experience."

Given the circumstances, that is, the change from Ragsdale's original tale to
his second, and the analysis by disinterested third parties, it would seem
that the Ragsdale testimony could be eliminated. It could be argued, however,
that the interference of Max Littell, and the attempts by the IUFOMRC to
obtain an "exclusive" story was the cause of the alteration. The first tale,
told under no inducement might be closer to the truth. Houran and Porter
thought that an analysis of the first tales might provide an insight into the
Ragsdale story.

Houran received a copy of the first affidavit and a copy of the Schmitt
interview with Ragsdale for analysis. Using the same techniques, they
reviewed the material. In the "Results and Discussion" section of their
report, Houran and Porter wrote, "...a free recall account is requisite
followed by a series of follow-up questions to do a competent assessment....
According to S.P. the problem with Ragsdale's 1993 testimony is that it is
completely non-focused, disjointed, and with no free recall account....
Consequently, conducting SVA on the present materials would not be productive
or meaningful...."

That wasn't the end, however. Houran and Porter wrote, "Having said this,
S.P. noted one glaring sign of non-credibility in this account, namely the
complete lack of description of any interactions between Ragsdale and his
companion. It is reasonable to expect that this would constitute a major part
of his narrative, given the novelty and bizarreness of the shared experience.
In our opinion there is also a clear "conspiratorial" air about the
interview.... Given our careful scrutiny of Ragsdale's testimony from both
1993 and 1995, we conclude that there is no evidence for its validity in a
forensic sense, and we recommend therefore that serious researchers discard
it."

From: KRandle993@aol.com

Good Morning, Tim -

>Thanks Kevin for the answer. I suppose the source is Frank Kaufmann.
>Perhaps you could elaborate on the document in question.

I suppose that now that Frank is dead, I'm not violating the confidence. He
provided a photocopy of the log he kept during these activities in New Mexico
in 1947. He had shown it to me several years before he provided the copy
and it provided the time and date. Given that it was a photocopy, the only
thing I could learn from it was that the typewriter was older than 1947 so it
could have been typed in that era. Certainly nothing there to rule it out a la
the Truman MJ-12 memo from a 1960s' typewriter.

I have but a single page, which, if Frank was inventing it, would have taken
him the better part of ten or twenty minutes to create. So, the document has
a provenance, which I suppose, is not particularly impressive, was created on
a typewriter that is, at least old enough, and has no real supporting
documentation
like the rest of the log.

As evidence proving Frank's involvement, or for convincing people of the
validity of
the event, it is very thin. Frank himself was aware of the trouble with
photocopied
material, telling me once, "Xerox is as loose as a goose," meaning that if
you had
a Xerox machine, you could easily manipulate the documents.

KRandle

From: Ktperehwon@aol.com
Date: Sun, 18 Nov 2001 16:16:37 EST
Subject: [UFORL] Curse of Corso

Dear Colleagues -- On Nov. 8, I attempted to post the message below on UFO
UpDates. Since then, I've retransmitted it to Errol twice--after adjusting
line length to be sure it conformed with his requirements. I've also
politely queried Errol, asking why he hadn't posted my message and what I
might do to adjust it to make it acceptable. I've had zero response from him
and, needless to say, my message remains unposted. Oddly, I receive UpDates
posts and have successfully posted other messages there, but on this issue...

So now I'm posting it here and on a couple of other lists. My intention was
to get the facts out on a very sleazy situation. I thought Errol to be
committed to the free exchange of ideas on UpDates. It appears I was wrong.
So now there's a second sleazy or at least highly questionable situation
here. I urge all who are interested/concerned, and regardless of their views
on Corso and Roswell in general, to re-post this anywhere they think it will
do some good and, if they're so inclinded, to ask Errol what gives. Of
course, he has the right to exclude what he wishes from his list, but given
what he HAS posted on this matter, I find it more than a little out of line
that he refuses to let my message see the light of virtual day on
UpDates--and a little common courtesy wouldn't hurt, even if it's to tell me
to buzz off. -- Cheers, KARL
----------------------
Fellow List Fiends --

In my book Roswell: Inconvenient Facts and the Will to Believe and in a 1997
MUFON Journal review of the late Lt. Col. Philip Corso's The Day After
Roswell (TDAR), I exposed the fact that Corso had pulled a bait and switch on
Senator Thurmond (R-SC), his former employer. Corso, who had worked for
Thurmond for two brief periods in the 1960s and '70s, had given the senator
an outline of his memoirs, grandly entitled I Walked With Giants (My Career
in Military Intelligence), asking him to pen a foreword for the book. The
senator did, and much to his chagrin, his brief, plain-vanilla
comments--laudatory of Corso but containing nothing specific about the book
itself--found their way into the first printing of TDAR.

When I saw the senator's name and foreword in the bound galleys of TDAR I was
sent by Simon & Schuster, Corso's publisher, I contacted his office.
Thurmond's staff was stunned, and in short order, the senator contacted S&S,
told them what had happened, and demanded that his foreword and name be
removed from further printings of the book and not be used in any way to
further promote it. The embarrassed publisher quickly complied.

The Oct.-Nov. 2001 UFO magazine (U.S.) carries a fatuous attempt to
rehabilitate Corso and, by implication, UFO's publisher William J. Birnes,
who coauthored TDAR with Corso: "Honor Restored: The 'De-Pflocked' Facts
About Philip Corso," by Don Ecker, the 'zine's director of research. Ecker
recently posted the text of this gem on UpDates, conveniently not including
the illustrations. The most important of these is a Simon & Schuster release
form signed by Senator Thurmond, allegedly giving his permission for Corso's
publisher to use his foreword in TDAR. The form as reproduced in UFO has the
words "Roswell Book" typed in the blank left in the boilerplate text of the
form for a book title, with the other blanks, for "undersigned" and "author,"
left, well, blank.

I made a copy of Ecker's piece available to Senator Thurmond's chief of
staff, and a few days ago, I received in return copies of several very
interesting items. One of these is the release form in the senator's office
file, on which ALL the blanks in text are, well, blank. No "undersigned," no
"author," but, most important, no book title, not even the generic "Roswell
Book." This clearly is the same form reproduced in UFO, as the senator's
signature and date of signing match--but it is as it was when the original
left the senator's office, BEFORE someone (gee, wonder who?) typed in
"Roswell Book." Hmmm...

Along with this revealing document, I received the complete outline for I
Walked With Giants, wherein nary a word about UFOs or Roswell (incident or
town) is found. A perusal of this outline and a reading of the senator's
foreword leave no doubt in any reasonable mind that the latter was intended
for the outlined proposed memoir, not the ufoological (NOT a typo) wet dream
to which it was appropriated. Other than the inclusion of many of the
non-UFO-connected tall tales and pulp-fiction prose that appeared in and
animated TDAR, the only resemblance between the proposed book and what
finally saw print is Corso's Walter Mittyish ego strutting across the pages.

Also included in the package were the senator's June 5, 1997, press release
about the matter ("Right Foreword, Wrong Book"), and his June 11, 1997,
letter to Simon & Schuster Deputy General Counsel Eric Raymond, demanding the
removal of his misappropriated foreword from TDAR.

I will not engage in further debate on this matter, on this list or in any
other forum, but will be glad to provide copies of any or all of these
documents to anyone who's interested enough to cover the cost of copying and
mailing. Those who'd like the full details of the Right Foreword, Wrong Book
Caper, will find them in chapter 16 of my book. Oh, and for what should be a
last laugh, don't miss the hilarious transcript of Paola Harris' July 5,

James, All -

>Aside from which, the foremost question remains how Kaufmann was

>existed and why would he compromise security by retaining his own

I thought I had made this clear. He did it the way it had always been done,
which is to say, after he finished the report, he physically wrote out a
second so that it looked as if he had retained an original copy. What he
showed me was clearly not made with carbon paper, another way to make
a copy prior to the photocopy machine.

It also strikes me that this could explain why the material he showed me
seemed
a little "thin." The copy he made for himself was a skeletal version of that
which he sent on to his superiors. I had hoped for more detail in the
information
he showed.

As for why he would compromise security by retaining the copies... and here
I must speculate... it could have been that he didn't believe the material he
retained compromised security because it didn't contain information that he
thought of as classified. The log has times and locations but little in the
way
of descriptive material. It's sort of a personal diary as opposed to a
detailed
log. Without Kaufmann to fill in the details, it really doesn't compromise the
security. As I say, this is speculation.

>Perhaps Kevin is now able to also clarify whether the 'log' he
>refers to contained the same material which Kaufmann produced for
>that 1995 'Incident at Roswell' documentary.

Frank showed me lots of documents, but I believe the material to which you
refer is from what he called his "Left hand sketch book." There were literally
dozens of drawing in it, many of them relating to the Roswell case, all of
them
looking as if they had been done years ago, but once again, not being allowed
to take the book for forensic testing, we're left with my admittedly untrained
eye. It looked as if the sketches were old, it looked as if the book was
filled
with the drawings that related and it looked as if this was something that
might
have taken a long time to complete.

From: James Easton <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Mon, 26 Nov 2001 09:36:34 +0000 (GMT)
Subject: [UFORL] Famous 'Wernher von Braun' UFO quotation

I'm sure the following will be of interest:

Date: 25 November 2001 22:51

Famous 'Wernher von Braun' UFO quotation
James Oberg

There is a widespread quotation attributed to Wernher von Braun
in 1959, apparently first printed by Timothy Good, as follows:

"We find ourselves faced by powers which are far stronger than we
had hitherto assumed, and whose base is at present unknown to us.
More I cannot say at present. We are now engaged in entering
into closer contact with those powers, and in six or nine months
time it may be possible to speak with some precision on the
matter." --This comment comes from "News Europa" Jan. 1959 and
refers to mysterious events during the re-entry phase of the Juno
2 rocket during a test flight.

One Internet example is
http://www.connect.net/mattvest/sciufo.htm

The reference is to the Pioneer-IV moon probe, launched by the
Army-built Jupiter IRBM with upper stages, in December 1958.

My colleague Tasillo Roemisch of SPACE SERVICE INTL. in
Mittweida, Germany, went to the Deutsche Buecherei in Leipzig and
found out the following:

The magazine 'NEUES EUROPA'(14 issues per year, all issues had
only 8 pages.) ceased publishing at the end of the sixties. Its
full title reads correctly: NEUES EUROPA. Das f hrende Weltblatt
fuer alle Fragen der kommenden Entwicklung. Verlag August Kraemer
GmbH, Stuttgart (New Europe. The leading World Magazine for all
questions of the coming development).

Roemisch checked all issues of the years 1959 and 1960 and found
out that they had been supporting a Karl Michalek who lived in
Santiago de Chile at that time and who claimed to be the
"President of the coming World Republic Earth". He was sure that
the Venusian ET's were going to land in Berlin soon. Furthermore
the writers often wrote about the well known UFO people George
Adamski and his associates.

Wernher von Braun was only mentioned one time, and that was in
issue no. 3 (Febr. 01, 1959) when they wrote that "Prof. Oberth,
the colleague of the German- American Wernher von Braun...
believes in the existence of extraterrestials living in the star
constallation Tau-Zeta, the Uranides."

The article footnoted by Good and so widely and trustingly
disseminated (issue no. 1, January 01, 1959, page 2) doesn't
mention von Braun at all. It read as follows. The headline was
"Sensationelle Zeichen aus dem Weltraum" (sensational signs from
outer space), and this is the sub-text: "Interplanetarische
Kr„fte, welche die irdischen Mond- Raketen aus ihrer Bahn lenken"
(interplanetary forces which direct terrestrial moon rockets out
of track), followed by "Russische und amerikanische Fern-
Raketen, die ihre Ziele nicht erreichen - Demonstration der
Venus- Kr„fte?" (Russian and American rockets which don't reach
their goals - demonstration of the Venusian forces?)

The article itself: Saturday Dec 06, 1958. Fourth attempt of the
USA moonrocket failed. Juno 2 was hindered in an altitude of
100,000 km to fly higher and came back. "Amerikanische
Sachverst„ndige betonen, dass es im Weltall Kr„fte gibt, welche
die irdischen Raketen aus ihren vorberechneten Bahnen ablenken,
ihre Fluggeschwindigkeit reduzieren und sie wieder in die
Lufth lle der Erde zur ckdirigieren." (American specialists
emphasize that there are forces in outer space to mislead
terrestial rockets out of their calculated tracks to reduce their
speed and to send them back to the atmosphere of the Earth)

The author was Albert Laurent and he claimed the Russian and
Indian researchers have said about the same.

As one would expect from an Adamski-ite rag, the real science and
technology was hopelessly garbled. The American moon probes had
followed gravitational trajectories with no outside interference
suspected, even then; instead, problems with the booster rockets
put them on the wrong initial courses.

This investigation of the actual rather than the distorted
'quotation' inaccurately attributed to Wernher von Braun is not
expected to have any impact on the false versions now extant on
the WWW.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Fri, 30 Nov 2001 00:13:57 -0000
Subject: [UFORL] Ufology and Demonology

During recent weeks I have been reading a new publication [2001
edition] of 'Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft', written by
Sir Walter Scott and originally published in 1830.

Some of the material Scott references is hugely insightful and
could be considered in a broader context, possibly relating to
contemporary 'encounters' with 'aliens' in more recent years.

Scott cites a number of cases where the observer had a clear,
sometimes lengthy, vision and how, significantly, this was
demonstrated to be borne of powerful imagination.

He notes that, "Somnambulism and other nocturnal deceptions
frequently lend their aid to the formation of such phantasmata as
are formed in this middle state, betwixt sleeping and waking".

Parallels with some tales of 'alien abduction'?

As a sceptical, yet eminently tolerant, treatise on the subject,
his writings are noteworthy to the extent I intended transcribing
several pages.

Fortunately, that will not be necessary as I have discovered the
entire publication is available on-line at:

http://www.sacred-texts.com/pag/scott/lodw00.htm

At the top of each page click on 'Next' or 'Previous'.


Although it's overall a lengthy commentary by Scott, each
'letter' is published with a preceding summary of its contents
and any points of related interest are easily found.

Whilst the earlier online publication contains an introduction by
Henry Morely, the latest introduction is by Dr. P. G. Maxwell-
Stuart, Honorary Lecturer at the University of St Andrews - see:

http://www.st-and.ac.uk/academic/history/modhist/staff/maxw.html

He writes: "Scott is not just presenting his readers with a crude
opposition between superstitious past and rational modernity. His
attitude towards the occult was more subtle than that, and his
acceptance of the nineteenth century's scientific claims was
tempered by reservation. As he wrote to Lady Louisa Stuart, 'Your
Ladyship cannot think me such an owl as to pay more respect to
Animal Magnetism or Scullology (I forget its learned name), or
any other _ology_ of the present day".

I wonder what Scott would have made of 'UFOs' as a 'present day'
_ology_.


I hope some subscribers might find Scott's letters of interest.


James Easton.
E-mail: voyager@ufoworld.co.uk
www.ufoworld.co.uk

<P>NASA's Mar's Global Surveyor has discovered evidence of what could be
described as 'the next step in the evolution of Mars.' </P>
<P>New observations show that the cold, dry, desert world is changing year by
year and may someday become a warmer and wetter environment, like scientists
suspect it was in its past. </P>
<P>These observations were made during a full Martian year, 687 Earth days. </P>
<P>"If the environment of Mars has really changed by as much and over as short a
time-scale as our observation implies, there should be attributes of Mars
reflecting these changes that may be measurable by landers," said Dr. Michael
Malin, principal investigator for Global Surveyor's camera system at Malin Space

For information, a copy of the cover can be see at:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/ftp/pilgrim.jpg


Also regarding:

>From: "Robinson, Larry" <lrobins@indiana.edu>
>To: <UFORL@yahoogroups.com>
>Subject: RE: [UFORL] 'Flying Saucer Pilgrimage'
>Date: 05 December 2001 00:16
Larry wrote:

>I have known about the Arnold "crescent" since the late 1960s or
>early 1970s. I will have to look and see where I found out about
>it.

Larry,

The 'crescent' [similar drawing as 'Flying Saucer Pilgrimage']
was on the cover of Arnold's own 1952 publication, 'The Coming of
the Saucers'.

I would be interested to know if Arnold ever publicised this
sketch [and also who created it for Arnold] before his book was
released.

Coincidentally, 'The Coming of the Saucers' seems to have been
reissued by 'Legend Press' - see:

http://www.bigbangco.com/ufomag/legendpress/

Alternatively, see:

http://members.aol.com/lgendpress/index.htm

Previously, the AOL 'Legend Press' home page confirmed that 'the
present Ray Palmer' was involved with this company.


"A few skeptics and scientists, however, voiced their
disapproval, but their protests were drowned out in the general
enthusiasm".

It could be a report from any recent UFO conference.

This, however, originates from one of the earliest - a lecture
given by George Adamski at the 400 seater Detroit Institute of
Arts, in 1954.

Such was the subsequent interest that Adamski reportedly stayed
on to give another lecture, selling 4,700 tickets at the Detroit
Masonic Temple!

I wonder if that's a record attendance for any UFO conference?

It's part of the fascinating story told in 'Flying Saucer
Pilgrimage' [1957], which is a rare insight charting the growth
of 'flying saucer' history through the experiences of sincere
enthusiasts, Bryant and Helen Reeve.
Despite their proclaimed skepticism, they were easily seduced by
Adamski's tales and those who followed in that vein.

No 'Roswell' related background - which wasn't of course
'rediscovered' until many years later - simply the first-hand
experience of figures who were fundamental in establishing
beliefs that not only were *saucer-shaped* spaceships visiting
earth, their *human-like* occupants were regularly making
contact.

I personally wasn't aware of all the contactees included therein
[this is the author's own timeline]:

George Adamski
Truman Bethurum
Dr. George Hunt Williamson
Desmond Leslie
Salvador Villanueva Medina [the Mexican 'Adamski']
George Van Tassel
Daniel Fry
Meade Layne
Mark Probert
Orfeo Angelucci


It was a highly commendable 1957 undertaking to discuss and offer
ostensibly scientific explanations for then key questions, such
as why only certain people were contacted, how could the visitors
travel for long periods through space, what was their propulsion
mechanism, did they believe in Jesus Christ and, most importantly
of course, could they cheat death.

Eventually, the contacts evolve into 'channelling', largely
featuring Mark Probert and the Inner Circle (sounds like a 50s
band).

Devoid of the scientific knowledge which only later became
available, some of the answers purportedly from the 'visitors'
are notable [questions from the authors]:

Q: How is it possible for beings like ourselves to live on other
planets of our solar system. How is this possible given the
different conditions of gravity, oxygen, pressure, etc?

A: Your scientific instruments are highly limited and do not
always give reliable information.

[...]

Venus is not as hot as many people think. It has a great band of
substance around it that protects it from much of the sun's
radiation. Mars is not an unhappy place to live. There is plant
life and animal life there besides human life.

Q: What about things falling out of the sky?

A: In your country, in California, not long ago and not too far
from this city (San Diego) huge blocks of ice fell down and
smashed some of your cars in the streets. The authorities, to
keep things quiet, said that this ice came from airplanes that
were being defrosted (laughter). They surely must have been
frozen in ice because some of the blocks weighed over 250 pounds!

My friends, where did this ice really come from? A body in space,
from Mars, from Venus? No. my friends, it came from what you
incorrectly call "empty space". Should space really open up, all
kinds of things would come out of it...

Q: What about the so-called "fire-balls"? Some are green fire-
balls.

A: The Guardians are doing all they can under cosmic law to help
men of earth. They send these great balls of light into the
atmosphere to help neutralize dangerous atomic radiations.
[END]


It's perhaps not unexpected that the authors and colleagues they
refer to as "experienced researchers" are completely taken in by
this!

An immensely enjoyable book and informative, albeit the stated
beliefs are, with hindsight, naive.

One surprise was to find the authors, in 1957, frequently refer
to the 'New Age' or 'Golden Age' and 'New Age young people'.

I didn't realise New Age beliefs were so old.


James Easton.

www.ufoworld.co.uk

In 'Flying Saucers Are Hostile', by Brad Steiger and Joan
Whritenour, the authors mention an incident involving "Ten-year-
old Sharon Stull of Albuquerque".

They write:

"Her case did, however, provoke an official response. Police
Chief A. B. Martinez issued an unprecedented warning to
Albuquerque residents, asking them to stay away from mysterious
objects. The law-enforcement official declined to state his views
on what the UFOs might be, but he strongly emphasized his warning
that "they should be treated with respect and caution".

Little Sharon Stull's doctor stated that he had found membrane
inflammation of both eyes and first-degree burns under the eyes
and on the nose. The physician had asked the girl to draw a
picture of the strange thing which had burned her with the
painful ray emanations. Sharon, and some playmates who had
witnessed the incident on April 28, 1964, told authorities that
the object had been shaped like an egg and was slightly smaller
than an airplane. They had seen no windows of any kind".

This was only four days after Lonnie Zamora's pivotal 'UFO'
encounter with an egg-shaped object, near Socorro.

Steiger and Whritenour make no allusions to any connection with
the Socorro event, possibly because of the time and distance
factors.

However, we now know there were some classified hot-air balloon
flights which had taken place in 1963 and extended into 1964,
launched from a site on the banks of the Rio Grande, north of
Albuquerque.

Although probably all merely coincidental and difficult to see
how the above reported injuries could have been caused by a hot-
air balloon, unless at extreme close proximity to its burner,
I've never come across the Sharon Stull story before now.

This must surely have generated publicity, perhaps even
investigation by APRO/NICAP and if any subscribers know more
about the background, I would be interested to hear from them.


As an aside, I submitted a Freedom of Information Act request in
search of the documents relating to those classified New Mexico
flights and any others which might be associated. I requested:

Any records pertaining to Office of Naval Research operations
involving experimental aircraft or balloon flights during the
years 1957-1964 inclusive. Specifically, those operations which
were carried out in conjunction with 'Raven Industries', of Sioux
Falls, South Dakota.

Instrumental in these flights was Ed Yost, one of the company's
founders and the foremost pioneer of ballooning.

involved with those Project Mogul balloon experiments which
almost certainly resulted in the Roswell 'flying saucer' debris
legacy.

The Langmuir web site confirms that, "Professor Moore retired
from his physics professorship at New Mexico Tech and gave up the
chairmanship of Langmuir Lab in late 1985. He continues as a
principal investigator of atmospheric physics at the lab".

Moore has commented on the Socorro case and I would be grateful
if anyone recalls his exact statement. If I remember, it was
something along the lines that he believed there were no hot-air
balloon flights in Socorro until many years later.

I've located the source of Prof. Moore's aforementioned statement
and believe this photograph can now be set in context. My thanks
to Karl Pflock for having previously obtained related background
information and making it available.

The balloon depicted is almost certainly a Raven model S-50,
which was an early prototype acquired by Prof. Moore from Ed and
J. R. Smith at Raven Industries in Sioux Falls.

It was used by Moore and Stirling Colgate to make test ascents
from the New Mexico Tech campus in Socorro and also by Moore for
some NSF-supported thunderstorm electrification experiments at
Langmuir Lab.

This was in 1967 and the basis of Moore's recollection that, so
far as he was aware, it was the first use of a hot-air balloon in
the Socorro area.

If a prototype balloon acquired by Moore maybe 2-3 years later,
it would explain why the platform design is so early - a wicker
basket was common by 1965.

What the Moore photograph does therefore potentially illustrate -
and the best example I've seen - is the likely type of platform
used by a circa 1964 hot-air balloon which Zamora might have
observed.

Bottom line; Prof. Moore has personally just reiterated: "There
is no way that anyone from Langmuir Lab was involved in a balloon
activity in New Mexico prior to 1965".

Appendix: An example of the disputes of 'fact' between UFOMag and
Oberg, regarding statements attributed to Scott Carpenter:

Misrepresentation of Astronaut Carpenter Quotation

ITEM: Mistreatment of Carpenter words and opinions regarding John
Glenn's "fireflies"

1. Narrator (~6 minutes into tape) refers to "curious anomalous
objects in orbit around earth", continues: "John Glenn likened
them to fireflies, and for a time, NASA actually believed they
had stumbled across living critters, according to one of its
retired astronauts, Scott Carpenter."

2. Stubbs on same tape at 44:30: "We have an astronaut making the
comment, on the 25th anniversary of the moon flight. He says,
it's hard to believe, but he says it's a FACT that we thought
that John's fireflies -- again, Glenn's fireflies -- were living
critters. Now at no time -- I've read everything -- at no time
have I ever heard that before, that NASA concluded originally
that the fireflies were alive."

3. Magazine article, March-April 2000, p. 8, account of Stubbs'
comments: "And we have an astronaut making a comment on the 25th
anniversary of the Moon flight where he says, 'It's hard to
believe, but it's a fact, that we thought that John's fireflies
were living critters'." [JimO: Note quotation marks]

4. Oberg's original note (March 20): refers to 'preposterous'
allegation that astronaut Scott Carpenter 'admitted' that NASA
for a long time thought that the 'fireflies' that Glenn reported
were 'living things'. I called it "a silly idea -- that Carpenter
would say such a thing", and asked for documentation outside of
somebody's vivid imagination.

5. Reply from Callaghan, March 21: we will "respond with the
video documentation that is absolutely proof positive that what
we claimed was said is the truth, and nothing but the truth."

6. Carpenter's actual quotation, as subsequently posted at UFOMag
website: "It's hard to realize this now, there were so many
unknowns in the early days, and this is a fact of the matter, we
were really not sure, after John flew, whether or not there were
critters, living critters up there somewhere."

7. Oberg responded that "the tape segment allegedly proving this
is pitifully ambiguous, doesn't even mention the fireflies, so I
suggest it was misinterpreted."

8. UFOMAG's reply: "[Oberg] challenged that we couldn't produce
any evidence to support our quotation of Scott Carpenter. We did,
and [Oberg] conceded the fact. Suggest [he] put that one to bed."

9. Not hardly! To repeat, Carpenter's posted quote in paragraph 3
(note that the transcript is not posted on the site, just the WAV
file for playing, which is a lot harder for most visitors) does
not mention 'fireflies' at all, and states NOT that people
'thought', 'believed', or 'concluded' anything, but that they
were not sure one way or the other about life in space somewhere.
The alleged quotation (paragraph 3) as printed in the magazine
inside quotation marks is clearly fraudulent and UFOMAG's
stubborn misrepresentation of it is indefensible on rational
grounds.

10. As for the big picture, aside from any genuine perplexity
about the phenomenon at the time it occurred, NASA very quickly
realized that the dots were ice particles coming from the
spacecraft's water spray boiler, which discarded waste heat from
the avionics (the space shuttle has a similar unit, called a
'Flash Evaporator', mounted at the base of the tail). Carpenter
himself confirmed this a few months later when on his flight he
was able to create swarms of 'fireflies' by banging on the side
of his capsule, where the water spray boiler was located. The
observed motion of the particles, falling below and pulling ahead
of the spacecraft, was exactly what is expected from high-drag
low-mass ice crystals. Today there is absolutely no basis in
reality to honestly portray the phenomenon as in any way
mysterious.
[END]


Perhaps this requires an updated definition of the 'abject
stupidity' boundaries which 'UFO' beliefs, especially commercial
enterprises, have encompassed, albeit there were precedingly no
limitations.

Kudos to Jim Oberg for even entertaining such purported
'scientific' garbage - or, if you prefer, "the most significant
cover-up evidence since Adamski, Trent, Roswell, MJ-12, Lazar, et
al...".
Every suggestion of an absurd "NASA cover-up" is so glaringly a
testimony to the absence of 'UFO' evidence in reality.


James Easton.

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Thu, 20 Dec 2001 00:28:58 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 'Socorro' Update

If Zamora had encountered a hot-air balloon, it was evidently
all-white and there certainly weren't many of those around at the
time.

Even rarer at that date was any balloon with a sizeable
manufacturer's emblem, or sponsorship logo.

Consequently, Zamora's reported 'insignia' remains one of the
peculiar aspects, which isn't helped by his discrepancies.

The related sketch he made, shown here:

http://www.qtm.net/~geibdan/a1999/mar/socorro2.jpg

...notably differs from the confirmation given to Chris Lambright
some years later:

http://www.cufon.org/contributors/chrisl/socorro.htm

I'm sure it was Joel Carpenter who pointed out that this
subsequent 'insignia' resembles the logo for Sandia National
Laboratories.

Conceivably some connection with the Sandia facility at
Albuquerque?

If not, there's perhaps more of a coincidence here than generally
realised.

Coral Lorenzen interviewed Zamora the day afterwards and in her
1966 book, 'Flying Saucers', wrote:

"The markings were in red, consisting of a vertical line topped
by two slanting lines that gave the impression of an arrow. This
was surrounded by a horizontal line on the bottom, a vertical
line on each side, and a semi-circle over the top of the arrow".

This is essentially as Zamora sketched for Chris Lambright, not
as he depicted on that earlier drawing.

It's also different from Zamora's sketches reproduced in 'Socorro
Saucer', by Ray Stanford. Again, these illustrate a semi-circular
arch covering the 'arrow', not "a vertical line on each side, and
a semi-circle over the top".
Did Sandia therefore have a comparative 'aerial vehicle' of some
kind in operation that day [Zamora's 'UFO' came from the
_general_ direction of ABQ] and was their current logo in use,
maybe coloured red, in 1964.

Although any connection seemed most unlikely, especially that
Sandia would, for some reason, be utilising a hot-air balloon in
1964, this was a possibility which strictly required to be
eliminated.

I had made due enquiries of Rebecca Ullrich, the Research
Historian at Sandia and Rebecca has been helpful in clarifying a
key issue. She writes:

"The Sandia logo has always been portrayed in turquoise. It did
change slightly in the early 1970s, so looked different in 1964
than it does now. The earlier version was more bird-like in
appearance and looked even less like the red image you've
provided than does the current logo".

I note there is in fact a copy of Sandia's original emblem on
their web site, at:

http://www.sandia.gov/recordsmgmt/oldtbird.gif

Rebecca has offered to investigate the matter further and that's
greatly appreciated.

However, it would seem we can surely rule out any link.


This returns the focus to limited options. Although some all-
white Raven hot-air balloons existed contemporary with the
Socorro case, there's currently no indication any of them would
have borne a symbol similar to Zamora's description.

Outwith Raven, circa 1964 some early hot-air balloon enthusiasts
and entrepreneurs constructed balloons for their own use, or by
others. Information on these is difficult to find so many years
later, although I know it does exist and there's one prime
candidate for an all-white balloon which did, at least in 1965,
contain a large 'bird' emblem, which isn't that dissimilar to
some of Zamora's drawings.

So far as Zamora's insignia, 'Sandia', as with 'International
Paper' - a logo which was also remarkably similar - certainly
seems to be a 'dead end'.

No surprise and many avenues of related research await,
hopefully, equally informative responses from potentially
significant sources.


James Easton.
E-mail: voyager@ufoworld.co.uk
www.ufoworld.co.uk

>

> Did Sandia therefore have a comparative 'aerial vehicle' of some
> kind in operation that day [Zamora's 'UFO' came from the
> _general_ direction of ABQ] and was their current logo in use,
> maybe coloured red, in 1964.

One of the things I wonder about in the Socorro case is just how
representative of the object Zamora's sketches really are. I don't know what
UFO investigators typically do, if anything, to make an assessment of
witness sketching ability. It seems that Lambright's effort here is pretty
exceptional.

I've been teaching an industrial design class for a few months at a local
school. The range of artistic talent the students exhibit is pretty broad,
even if they have good creative abilities. It seems that sketches done by
people without formal training are essentially lists of notable features of
objects rather than exact representations.

I can't recall ever seeing a sketch of a crime suspect that was done by an
actual police officer. But police sketch artists can work with a witness
through verbal instructions to produce remarkably accurate sketch of a
person. Look at the Unabomer drawing, for example.

A thought experiment: Zamora is in his car chasing the speeder when the
Soviet Lunar Module

http://www.friends-partners.org/mwade/craft/lk.htm

drops out of the sky and lands near the road. He drives toward it, sees it
from a distance - a cosmonaut is standing next to it - and just as he gets
near it, it blasts off and zooms away.

Take a good look at it -- it would have been impossible for him (or any
witness) to make an accurate sketch of something that complex under those
circumstances. What you might get would be something similar to what he
actually drew. You could visualize the same scenario using other manmade
objects like Harrier jets, Apache helicopters, etc, and try to guess what
the resulting sketch might look like.

The only way you could try to take this problem into account would be to
sort of calibrate the drawing ability of the witness by asking him or her to
draw something familiar. In Zamora's case, I'd say, "please draw your police
car, with yourself standing beside it in scale with the car." Nothing fancy
- give the witness about 5 minutes tops. If you can identify the type of
car, you're doing great. If the self-portrait is more than a stick figure,
it's even better. Then you might do something along other lines, like
showing him photos of something like the Lunar Module, an F-14 fighter, a
balloon, etc, for a few seconds at a time and asking him to quickly sketch
them. This would provide some basis for assessing the abilities of the
particular witness to assimilate details of complex vehicles quickly and
reproduce them accurately. (You might also test color perception).

I say all this because I suspect that Zamora's sketch is highly stylized and
oversimplified. For instance, there's no indication of pads on the ends of
the little stick-figure legs, but they must have been there (unless they're
balloon marks, but I'll get back to that). I just have a feeling that the
actual object was not just a featureless white ellipsoid with a big red logo
on the side. If Zamora drew his patrol car test drawing like a little kid's
sketch of a car -- a small box on a big box with a star on the door and oval
wheels, you'd know that this is just how he represents everything, not just
UFOs. But this experiment should have been done over 35 years ago...

I think it's foolish to take witness sketches too literally -- like Barney
Hill's drawing of the Leader, with his cap and huge eyes. You could go to
extremes -- looking for caps that were common in the Boston area in the
early 60s, measuring them, comparing the diameter of the cap to the size of
the eyes and then speculating about the refractive index of the atmosphere
on their home world ... but it's really not useful, is it? The sketch is
obviously a kind of symbolic representation where the eyes are huge because
of their emotional significance.

I still think Zamora's object was a UFO, unidentified, not a balloon. I
suspect it was a manmade vehicle, but I don't know what the culprit actually
was. I've expressed my doubts about this before and I won't belabor it.

Joel

From: "James Easton" <voyager@ufoworld.co.uk>
Date: Mon, 24 Dec 2001 02:54:07 -0000
Subject: Re: [UFORL] 'Socorro' Update

Regarding:

>From: "joel carpenter" <ufx1947@home.com>
>To: <UFORL@yahoogroups.com>

Joel wrote:

>I still think Zamora's object was a UFO, unidentified, not a
>balloon. I suspect it was a manmade vehicle, but I don't know
>what the culprit actually was. I've expressed my doubts about
>this before and I won't belabor it.

Joel,

This perhaps implies the reasons expressed for those doubts
remain significant obstacles to a hot-air balloon being
responsible.

In fact, all of the stated reasons have been duly addressed.

A main objection cited, not only by your good self, was data
which confirmed the wind was blowing in an opposite direction to
the object's arrival and departure.

When researched further, it turned out there evidently wasn't any
such data obtained during the initial case investigations.

The background to this was explained in 'Voyager' newsletter No.
18 - see:

http://www.ufoworld.co.uk/v18.txt

Other doubts expressed concerned Zamora's perception of the
object's size. This was also discussed in the publication and I
pointed out that Chris Lambright's sketch, which Zamora confirmed
as accurately representative [it's of course 'subjective' and
comes back to the difficulties you raised about witness
sketches], depicted an object which was larger than a hot-air
balloon.


The 'ground markings' were a further apparent discrepancy,
claimed to be inconsistent with a balloon's platform. The object
had seemingly landed, not dragged along the ground as a hot-air
balloon would.

Yet, once again, when duly researched it was discovered
otherwise, as I explained in the newsletter:

If it was a hot air balloon, then any landing would not have been
a 'touchdown' and the balloon's platform is likely to have
dragged along the ground, even for a short distance.

At this time, it seems that an extremely basic, rectangular
wooden or metal platform with 'railings' was gradually being
superseded by the more familiar wicker basket.

The 'official' case investigator was Dr J. Allen Hynek, former
Chairman of the Astronomy Department at Northwestern University
and who became a consultant for the US Air Force's 'Project Blue
Book'.

In a private memo dated 20 May, 1964, Hynek wrote that, contrary
to the landing marks being 'impressions', they were in fact, "4
rectangular scrapings as if a rectangular object had scraped
along digging into the ground" and that "the gouging was done
away from the center in every case".

There is a photograph, published in several books, which shows
one of the 'imprints' and the rocks which had been placed around
to protect this presumed 'trace evidence'. As one of Richard
Hall's colleagues further commented:

"It shows several small rocks protruding _in situ_ from the
crater as if they belonged there but now are exposed -- so they
could not simply have been accidentally kicked in by
investigators from the surrounding soil outside of the landing
print. These small rocks have obviously _not_ been pressed down
into the bowl shape of the crater by any 'great weight'. A 'great
weight' would have pushed the small rocks down into the soil so
that their tops would have been flush or almost flush with the
contour of the crater, and they most likely would have been
crushed or broken -- but they are not pushed down or broken. The
imprints look like they have been dug or gouged out exactly as
Hynek said, _not_ pressed down by a massive object".

Once again, the facts are somewhat different from those published
in UFO lore.
[END]


Also highlighted by yourself and others, was that Major Hector
Quintanilla of Project Blue Book had thoroughly investigated the
case. Why then, did he overlook this explanation?
Primarily of course because no-one had seemingly considered the
object perhaps wasn't metallic, emitting a downwards jet of
flame.

However, it appears there were at least two glaring omissions in
that supposedly 'thorough' investigation. The first, as discussed
and evidently confirmed on this list's predecessor, 'UFO
Skeptics', was how no-one had contacted the nearby Socorro
airport to enquire if they knew of anything flying in the area at
that time.

The second is one which I've never seen mentioned before now.

There was another potential, first-hand witness and it seems he
was never interviewed. Incredible, as he probably had a clearer
view of the object than Zamora did as it came in to land.

This witness was the 'speeder' Zamora was pursuing when Zamora
first heard that loud roar and observed a slowly descending
flame. As he wrote in his official report:

About 5:45 P.M. 4/24/64 while in Socorro 2 Police Car (64 Pontiac
white) started to chase a car due south from west side of Court
House. Car was apparently speeding, and was about 3 blocks in
front. At point on Old Rodeo Street (extension of Park St. south)
near George Morillo residence (about 1/8 mile south of Spring
Street, the _____ chased car was going straight ahead toward
rodeo grounds. Car chased was a new black Chevrolet (it might
have been _____ boy about seventeen). Chased car still about
three blocks ahead. _____ alone.

At this time heard a roar and saw a flame in the sky to southwest
some distance away--possibly a 1/2 mile or a mile. Came to mind
that a dynamite shack in that area had blown up, decided to leave
chased car go.

[...]

Flame about twice as wide at bottom as top, and about four times
as high as top was wide. Did not notice any object at top, did
not note if top of flame was level. Sun was to west and did not
help vision. Had green sun glasses over prescription glasses.
Could not see bottom of flame because it was behind the hill.

[...]

No other spectators noted--no traffic except the car in front--
and car in front might have heard it but possibly did not see it
because car in front was too close to hill in front, to see the
flame".
[END]

The 'speeder' may not have had a good view of the flame as it
disappeared behind the hill, however, he might have clearly
observed the flame and more significantly what it originated
from, beforehand.

This wasn't a mystery witness who, understandably, didn't come
forward or could never be traced. It's documented that Zamora
knew the speeder's almost certain identity, which in 'Socorro
Saucer' Ray Stanford notes wasn't that difficult in a small town.

I dare say this potential witness, if alive and especially still
resident in Socorro, could yet be interviewed.

So far as I'm aware, that didn't happen during Quintilla's
investigation.


Those expressed doubts are understood, however, they have never
been overlooked! Surely though, some, if not all, of them are no
longer valid.


Aside from Hynek's own evidence that the object "scraped along"
the ground when it landed, we know its propulsion was an
intermittent, roaring flame which Zamora confirmed did not impact
on the ground as the vehicle departed and it did not 'take off'
straight upwards, instead slowly gaining altitude at a 'shallow
angle'. The 'UFO' could also still do [and escape Earth's
gravity] when the initial propulsion was switched off.

Except for a hot-air balloon, I'm not aware of any other "manmade
vehicle" which has these characteristics or, as Zamora radioed
when said object departed in the distance, "looks like a
balloon".


One factor I have personally built into the 'equation' was a
remaining 'objection' - how is it conceivable Zamora could not
have recognised the object was a hot-air balloon, or, eventually
realised this when he, doubtless, had at least seen photographs
or film of them in later years. Wouldn't Zamora subsequently have
publicised the likely explanation?

So far as the latter goes, evidently not in a zillion light
years.

A fascinating, informed insight into this was offered by Thomas
Guengerich, editor and publisher of local newspaper, the 'El
Defensor Chieftain'.

I haven't revealed it publicly until now.

Let's just say that Guengerich, who knows Zamora - as do "several
people on my staff" - set that issue, and some others, in the
context of 'local knowledge'.


Is the hot-air balloon conclusion shared by those with relevant
expertise *and* who are aware of the facts when comprehensively
detailed...

Don Piccard, along with Ed Yost, was largely responsible for the
development of hot-air ballooning. He concludes:

"I would take the position that your surmises are correct and
that the case is closed. Any further investigation could be
considered tilting at windmills".

Jim Winker was Vice-President of Raven Industries and worked with
the company during the first 35 years of its existence. The
first, modern, hot air balloon flight took place on October 22,
1960 and there's a relatively well known photograph of this
event. Until recently, I didn't appreciate that Jim Winker had
taken this photograph, as noted on celebrated British balloonist
Julian Nott's web site:

http://www.nott.com/favorite_balloon_flights.htm,

Jim Winker concludes of 'Socorro':

"I can't do much but agree that all evidence points to a hot air
balloon".


I would contend that is by any default the proverbial bottom
line.

The evidence is considerable and certainly opposed to the
seemingly total absence of same as regards another man-made
candidate, overwhelming.

The ultimate proof, obviously subject to ongoing research, must
naturally be 'out there' - is that perhaps, in fact, the only
remaining challenge?

Alternatively, what is the factual basis for any lingering, 'no
way'?
